    FSC peers¶

    The FSC group fsc-demo runs OpenFSC v2.4.0. Each organization has its own FSC components, a txlog API, and a Peer ID. A self-hosted directory peer and certificate portal serve the group. The group has these peers:

    Organization Peer ID Units Role
    Directory peer …0000 directory-manager, directory-inway, directory-controller, directory-txlog-api, directory-ui Group registry. It signs service publications automatically. It signs nothing else.
    EDI issuer (GBO) …0100 edi-manager, edi-outway, edi-controller, edi-txlog-api Consumer for EUDI issuance (bri, brp) and for the metadata services. The EUDI rules list it as a designated issuer.
    Belastingdienst mock …0200 bd-manager, bd-inway, bd-controller, bd-txlog-api Provider of bri, brp (RvIG), lvg, gbo-metadata-bd, and gbo-metadata-rvig. Its Manager decides contracts through the PDP. Its Inway is the PEP.
    Mortgage lender mock (Hypotheek-BV) …0300 hv-manager, hv-outway, hv-controller, hv-txlog-api DvTP consumer of bri
    BRP/RvIG mock …0400 brp-manager, brp-inway, brp-controller, brp-txlog-api Provider peer with its own PEP and contract decision. The default demo publishes RvIG on …0200 instead. make fsc-seed-brp publishes brp here.
    Consent register (GBO) …0700 cr-manager, cr-inway, cr-controller, cr-txlog-api Provider of consent-status. The Inway has no AuthZEN hook. The Manager decides contracts through the PDP.
    PDP (GBO) …0800 pdp-manager, pdp-outway, pdp-controller, pdp-txlog-api Consumer of consent-status
    Installatie Register …1000 ir-manager, ir-outway, ir-controller, ir-txlog-api DvTP consumer of lvg
    Integrator (opt-in) …1100 int-* (profile integrator) Delegated consumer of bri for Hypotheek-BV
    ASIP (GBO, opt-in) …1200 asip-manager, asip-outway, asip-controller, asip-txlog-api (profile asi) Consumer of brp on …0200 with grant link /brp. The admission register lists it as a system participant.

    One FSC peer can host more than one logical source. In the default demo, the RvIG and LVG sources use the Belastingdienst peer …0200 and its OIN. Each source still has its own service, gateway, metadata document, and certificate set. This shared peer is a demo shortcut. The demo therefore does not show one OIN per bronhouder (REQ-67).

    ASI units¶

    The asi profile runs these units:

    Unit Host port (container) Networks Notes
    asi-provider 9424 (4020) backend, fsc-infra, eudi Reads the source registry with the reader role. Uses asip-outway.
    asi-authorization-server 9425 (4021) backend Keeps clients, codes, and transactions in memory
    asi-wallet-verifier 9428 (8001), internal API 8002 backend Needs the nl-wallet sources. A real wallet needs HTTPS, through a tunnel.
    asi-discovery-stub 9426 (4022) backend External role, stub
    qtsp-reference 9427 (4023) backend, eudi External role, demo scaffolding

    One-shot jobs¶

    The chart renders a task as a Job (job.enabled: true). The source registry bootstrap, the source registry migrations, and the issuance migrations are Jobs. A database lock or one transaction stops a second copy of a Job from running at the same time. The issuance configuration materializer is an init container. It writes issuance_server.toml into an emptyDir for each pod. postgres-eudi is a Deployment with Recreate and a ReadWriteOnce volume.

    The rollout order is bootstrap, then migrations, then the reconciler, the adapter, and the issuance server (chart README).

    Certificates and PKI¶

    FSC traffic is mTLS inside a self-generated PKI. cfssl serves a root CA and an intermediate CA, with a certificate portal for CSRs. Each organization gets a group certificate with its OIN in serialNumber and its name in O. It also gets internal mTLS certificates (fsc-infra/pki). The legal identity of an organization comes from its certificate (REQ-67).

    Private keys are not in Git. Each checkout generates them again.

    The EUDI and ASI material comes from two pre-provisioned development CAs: an issuer CA and a reader CA. The Makefile refuses to generate them. A separate privileged command mints leaf certificates under them. The runtime gets leaves and public CA certificates. It never gets a CA private key. The demo has the following certificate and key material:

    Material Minted by (demo) Held at runtime by Production
    FSC group and internal certificates, per organization fsc-infra/pki bootstrap scripts (cfssl) The FSC components of that organization PKIoverheid (REQ-46)
    PDP AuthZEN TLS certificate generate-pdp-cert.sh PDP. Inways and Managers pin it as CA. Platform TLS (Helm: Secret openftv-pdp-tls)
    Consent proof signing key Consent register at start, or a mounted file (CONSENT_SIGNING_KEY_PATH, required with a persistent store) Consent register Managed key. Key rotation is an open question (Q-55).
    Source decryption keys Demo keys in the gateway image, for the shared demo OIN Source gateway and decryption component. A deployment mounts its own keys (SUBJECT_KEYS_DIR). BSNk key delivery per source (BSNK-09). Old key versions stay available as long as consent proofs that use them are valid (AV-09).
    EUDI certificate set per source: issuer, reader, status list make provision-development-certificates Issuance server (private keys through the init step) and reconciler (public leaves only) Qualified seal certificate in a QSCD, access and registration certificates, and a status-list certificate. Key custody is an open question (Q-17).
    Reference QTSP issuance set: reader, issuer, status list, callback TLS make provision-qtsp-issuance-certificates Issuance server, reference QTSP Outside GBO. The QTSP holds its own set.
    ASIP seal certificate make provision-asip-seal-certificate (issuer CA) ASIP Qualified seal certificate. It is open who holds it (Q-28, ADR-0041).
    QTSP client certificate make provision-asip-qtsp-certificate (reader CA) Reference QTSP Wallet-relying-party access certificate (Q-35)
    Wallet verifier reader certificates (asi-login, qtsp-login) make provision-asi-wallet-verifier (reader CA) Wallet verifier Access certificate
    ASI authorization server signing key If AZSP_SIGNING_KEY_FILE is not set, the server makes an ephemeral key at start. Authorization server Managed key

    Missing or incomplete EUDI material blocks only that source (REQ-58). The issuance server trusts the pre-production NL PID issuer CA. Its PID trust list also holds the development issuer CA and the issuer CA of every source. This list is too broad (REQ-45). The ASI wallet verifier trusts a fixed list: the pre-production PID issuer and the development issuer CA. Neither list is the EU Trusted List.

    Production needs separate certificate roles per bronhouder for EUDI: access, registration, qualified seal, and status list. It is open which trust list anchors PuB-EAA providers (Q-30). Identity and trust and ADR-0023 explain the roles.

    Data stores¶

    GBO and the demo keep data in these stores:

    Store Backing Content
    Consent register In memory by default. Postgres is optional. Consent records and the portal's PI and PP per subject_ref (REQ-69). No BSN, no VI, and no VP.
    Admission register SQLite volume dvtp-onboarding-data Participants and integrator mandates
    Authorization Decision Log Postgres postgres-ftv, database ftv_adl, in every profile. Readers use the SELECT-only role adl_reader. One record per PDP evaluation (REQ-71)
    OpenFTV Manager (opt-in) Same postgres-ftv instance Policies and the bundle
    LDV logbooks Seven SQLite volumes logboek-*-data Processing records per controller (REQ-72)
    LDV outboxes Volume ldv-outbox-* per writer Records that wait for delivery to the logbook
    FSC txlogs Postgres in fsc-infra, one database per peer Transport records
    Issuance server session store Postgres postgres-eudi Wallet session state
    Source registry Postgres postgres-eudi, schema source_registry, writer and reader roles Candidates, statuses, immutable releases (snapshot 3.0, or 4.0 with asi), and the active-release pointer
    Issuance runtime Volume eudi-issuance-runtime issuance_server.toml, written from the active release
    Source documents (file transport) Read-only mount source-metadata/ Operator-managed descriptions for sources without an endpoint
    GBO attribute catalog schemas/asi-attributes.json value_schema per ASI attribute identifier
    ASI state In memory, plus a register stub file Registrations, codes, and transactions of the authorization server. Logins and pending statements of the reference QTSP.
    Jaeger, Loki Volumes, seven-day retention Debug traces and logs, including the engine's console decision log

    Observability and audit stores¶

    The stores fall into two groups with different duties (logging):

    • Audit stores hold the authoritative records: the ADL for decisions, the LDV logbooks for processings, and the FSC txlogs for transport (REQ-32). Each peer has its own txlog API. This includes the GBO peers cr, pdp, and asip.
    • Observability stores are for debugging. An OpenTelemetry collector receives OTLP from all services. It exports to Jaeger and to the developer portal's live event stream. Promtail ships container logs to Loki, including the engine's console decision log. Grafana shows dashboards. These stores are never the record of a decision.

    One W3C trace ID per request joins the records. The FSC transaction ID is recorded next to it (ADR-0035). On the simulation platform, one observability stack runs in MinEZK, and MinBZK shares it (OBSERVABILITY.md). In demo v0.9.0, no audit store has a retention policy, an access model, or tamper evidence (Q-08).

    Availability model¶

    The demo is built for inspection. Availability is not one of its goals. The demo-grade choices in the following lists must change for production. Risks and technical debt tracks them.

    Authorization and consent have these demo-grade choices:

    • One PDP serves all providers. The target is a PDP per bronhouder (ADR-0004). The PDP does not start without its ADL database, so postgres-ftv runs in every profile.
    • Every DvTP decision needs the consent status, live, over FSC. By default, the register keeps its data in memory. Production needs a replicated store and an availability target for this role (REQ-75).
    • The PDP pulls the admission register every 5 s. If the register is missing, the PDP denies contracts with ADMISSION_REGISTER_UNAVAILABLE. It denies delegated calls with INTEGRATOR_REGISTER_UNAVAILABLE.
    • The LDV logbooks are off the critical path. If a logbook is down, the outbox delays the record. The request still completes.

    EUDI issuance has these demo-grade choices:

    • The issuance server reads its configuration at start. After a change of the active release, the server needs a controlled restart (state rollout_required).
    • If one source is outside its stale grace period, it blocks new releases for all sources. Then the offer catalog answers 503 for all sources (REQ-66).
    • The adapter callback must be reachable over public HTTPS. It needs caller authentication (REQ-45).

    The ASI chain has these demo-grade choices:

    • The authorization server keeps registrations in memory. After a restart, every QTSP registers again. Without AZSP_SIGNING_KEY_FILE, issued tokens also stop working after a restart.
    • If the register is unreachable at a re-check, the client stays active (Q-34).
    • If the current source description or the keys of the authorization server are missing, the ASIP fails closed (503).

    In production, the mocked services become external dependencies with their own availability: BSNk, DigiD, and the register of relying parties.

    Traceability¶

    • Requirements: REQ-32, REQ-45, REQ-39, REQ-46, REQ-58, REQ-66, REQ-67, REQ-69, REQ-71, REQ-72, REQ-75, REQ-76, REQ-81, BSNK-09, AV-09
    • Findings: F-42 (closed), F-79 (open)
    • Open questions: Q-08, Q-17, Q-28, Q-30, Q-34, Q-35, Q-55, Q-58
    • Demo increments: SL-10, SL-26, SL-28, SL-34, SL-34a, SL-34b, SL-34c, SL-35, SL-36, SL-37, SL-49

    Crosscutting concepts

    Authorization¶

    GBO authorizes every data request with policy-based access control. A policy engine decides, and the FSC Inway of the source enforces the decision. The authorization model on this page is the model that gbo-demo v0.9.0 builds. The model realizes capability S05.

    The model follows from seven architecture decisions:

    • ADR-0002: OPA/Rego in OpenFTV, the FSC Inway as PEP, and AuthZEN with the FTV GraphQL profile.
    • ADR-0004: five concerns, federated evaluation, and no central authorization server.
    • ADR-0009: closed-world rules, bound by regime and service.
    • ADR-0013: the request mapper only maps.
    • ADR-0015: FSC contract acceptance by policy.
    • ADR-0031: the regime follows from the evidence.
    • ADR-0032: the policy verifies the consent proof.

    For the consent proof, see Consent. For how the source fills in the citizen after the decision, see Pseudonymization. For how policy gets to the PDP, see Policy lifecycle.

    Five concerns¶

    Authorization answers five separate questions. Each question has its own decision maker, protocol, and moment. Each concern has its own enforcement point:

    # Concern Question Enforced by
    ① Organization identity Is this a legitimate organization? mTLS with PKIoverheid certificates at every FSC connection (Identity and trust)
    ② Organization permission Can this organization use this service? FSC contract and access token, issued by the FSC Manager of the provider. Contract acceptance is a policy decision on the admission register (Admission and contract acceptance)
    ③ Access basis Is there a consent, or a verified PID of the citizen? PDP policy: the regime follows from the evidence (Regime selection). The policy verifies the consent proof and gets the status online (Consent verification in policy). The design has a Gov-to-Gov regime on a legal basis. Demo v0.9.0 does not build it
    ④ Data scope Which fields, records, and years can the source return? PDP policy: per-field rules, the subject placeholder, and the year filter (Rule model)
    ⑤ Request validity Is the request well-formed and complete? Request mapper: FTV GraphQL profile, limits, and schema pins (Query mapping). The source gateway accepts only the judged request shape. Demo v0.9.0 does not build rate limiting (Risks)

    No central authorization server exists. Concerns ① and ② are in the FSC layer, federated per organization. The PDP of the source evaluates concerns ③ to ⑤ for each request. With the integrator path, concern ② also has a part at request time: the mandate check (ADR-0034).

    PEP, PDP, PIP¶

    flowchart LR C[Consumer Outway] -->|mTLS + FSC token| IN subgraph SRC[Bronhouder] IN[FSC Inway = PEP] subgraph PDP[OpenFTV PDP v0.1.0] MAP[FTV GraphQL mapper] POL[Rego policy] end OUT[PDP Outway] GW[Source gateway<br/>bron-sidecar] API[Source API] end REG[(Admission register)] CR[(Consent register)] IN -->|AuthZEN evaluation, raw body| MAP MAP -->|field list| POL POL -->|status over FSC| OUT OUT --> CR POL -.->|JWKS, cached| CR REG -.->|PIP pull every 5 s| POL IN -->|only after allow| GW GW --> API %% GBO diagram palette: the same colors as the Globaal Ontwerp classDef basis fill:#DCFCE7,stroke:#16A34A,color:#0F172A classDef dvtp fill:#FEDCD8,stroke:#E28F80,color:#1E293B classDef eudi fill:#FFEDD5,stroke:#EA580C,color:#0F172A classDef source fill:#DDEBF7,stroke:#6F94B8,color:#1E293B classDef ext fill:#F1EFE8,stroke:#5F5E5A,color:#444441 classDef store fill:#EDE9FE,stroke:#7C3AED,color:#1E1B4B classDef mock fill:#F3F4F6,stroke:#9CA3AF,color:#374151,stroke-dasharray:4 3 classDef planned fill:#FFFFFF,stroke:#9CA3AF,color:#6B7280,stroke-dasharray:6 4 classDef zoom stroke-width:3px class C,IN,MAP,POL,OUT,GW basis class API source class REG store class CR dvtp style SRC fill:#FFFFFF,stroke:#6F94B8,stroke-dasharray:4 3 style PDP fill:#F4F5F7,stroke:#16A34A

    The components in the diagram have these roles:

    • The PEP is the FSC Inway of the source. Its AuthZEN plugin sends every request, with its raw body, to the PDP. The plugin forwards the request only on allow (fsc-infra/docker-compose.yml#L769-L775). No separate PEP service exists (F-35). The PEP passes the request unchanged and never parses it (REQ-42).
    • The PDP is OpenFTV release v0.1.0 with embedded OPA/Rego. The demo builds it from the tag and patches in the FTV GraphQL mapper (Dockerfile#L3-L9). The mapper builds the field list and does nothing else (ftvgraphql.go#L1-L13). It does not verify consent, does not call BSNk, and reads no flow. The policy establishes every fact that it decides on (REQ-18).
    • PIP 1 is the consent register (toestemmingsregister). During evaluation, the policy calls the register for the status of the consent. The call goes over FSC, through the own Outway of the PDP (docker-compose.yml#L141-L142). The policy gets the verification keys (JWKS) directly from the register.
    • PIP 2 is the admission register. Every 5 seconds, OpenFTV pulls the participants as data.entities.dvtp_participant. Each participant has the attributes name, active, allowed_source_peer_ids, and acts_for (dvtp-onboarding.yaml). The contract policy reads this data. The request policy reads it for integrator mandates (acts_for).

    The same PDP serves two enforcement points. Each point has its own policy tree. FSC Inways send data requests (package authz). FSC Managers send contract proposals (package doelbinding.auto_sign_contract).

    The EUDI adapter and the ASIP call the source over FSC, like every other consumer. They translate between protocols. The decision on source data stays with the PDP of the source (REQ-44).

    The source gateway is behind the Inway. Only the Inway can reach the gateway. As a result, the gateway does all its work after the decision (REQ-04, ADR-0033).

    Regime selection¶

    The PDP judges a request under one of two regimes. The evidence in the request selects the regime (REQ-74, ADR-0031). A declared regime plays no part. Each kind of evidence has its own outcome:

    Evidence in the request Regime Rules that bind
    One X-GBO-Consent-Token, verified or not consent DVT0001, LVG0001
    No consent token PID EUD0001, EUD0002, ASI0001
    Two consent tokens — denied: CONSENT_CONTEXT_INVALID

    The selection code is in engine.rego#L168-L181. The code that reads the token is in consent.rego#L44-L62. FSC grants carry no properties. No component reads a flow.

    The regime only decides which reasons the PDP reports. Access depends on the rules, because each rule still checks its own basis. If no verified consent is present, DVT0001 denies. If a consent token is present, the PID rules deny.

    Only consent is positive evidence (F-70). A request enters the PID regime because no token is present. This asymmetry has two consequences:

    • The PID regime needs its own positive evidence: a verified PID disclosure, bound to the subject of the query (REQ-45). In demo v0.9.0, the EUDI adapter does not authenticate the callback that carries the PID (#133).
    • The actor lists of the PID rules (designated_issuers, asip) must stay disjoint from the consent consumers in every environment. If the lists overlap, a consumer can skip consent: it leaves out the token. A test checks this condition for the seeded peers only (engine_test.rego#L366-L376).

    A Gov-to-Gov regime on a legal basis needs its own positive evidence. It cannot be a third regime that the absence of evidence defines.

    Wallet approval is not a legal basis¶

    In DvTP, the consent of the citizen is the legal basis for delivery to a private consumer. In the EUDI route, the citizen chooses in the wallet which data to present. The ARF says that this approval is never a legal basis for the relying party (F-83). In the ASI route, the citizen approves each request by logging in (REQ-90). This approval is not a stored, revocable consent either.

    As a result, no single "consent" covers all routes. The PID regime cannot use a DvTP consent as its basis. The consent regime cannot use a wallet presentation as its basis. If a consumer gets data both through DvTP and through the wallet, it needs its own legal basis for the wallet route. The GO and the PSA do not separate the two terms.

    Rule model¶

    Each rule is a plain Rego package under policies/gbo/rules/ (ADR-0009). A rule declares three things:

    • rule_id, regime (consent or pid), and services (the FSC services that the rule applies to).
    • covers_fields and covers_types: the fields that the rule can grant.
    • Its reasons to refuse: deny for the whole request and deny_field[i] for one field.

    If a rule gives no reason, it grants the field. Each rule checks actor and scope itself (REQ-48). The file lib.rego only reads the request and holds no checks.

    Demo v0.9.0 has five rules:

    Rule Regime Service What it grants Own reasons to refuse
    DVT0001 consent bri Income declaration fields under consent consent codes, SCOPE_NOT_ALLOWED, CONSTRAINT_MISMATCH, YEAR_NOT_COVERED, CONSENT_ACTOR_MISMATCH
    LVG0001 consent lvg Ownership check at the LVG, scope lvg:vbo:eigendom consent codes, SCOPE_NOT_ALLOWED, CONSTRAINT_MISMATCH
    EUD0001 pid bri Income statement (inkomensverklaring) to the wallet, years 2024 and 2025 PID_NOT_PRESENT, ACTOR_NOT_ALLOWED, YEAR_NOT_ALLOWED
    EUD0002 pid brp Death certificate (akte van overlijden) to the wallet PID_NOT_PRESENT, ACTOR_NOT_ALLOWED
    ASI0001 pid brp BRP fields for the ASIP PID_NOT_PRESENT, ACTOR_NOT_ALLOWED

    The consent codes are the outcomes of the proof verification and the status lookup. For more information, see Consent verification in policy.

    How the engine binds rules to fields¶

    The engine (engine.rego) decides each data field of the field list separately, in these steps:

    1. Only the rules of the active regime bind.
    2. Only the rules that serve the FSC service of the request bind (REQ-97). The service is the service_name from the FSC access token. The Manager of the source signed this token (engine.rego#L183-L192).
    3. A field binds to the rules that name its key ParentType.field. An argument-free leaf outside the root types also binds to the rules that cover its parent type.
    4. Every delegated call needs an integrator mandate for the represented party and the granting rule (engine.rego#L246-L267). The engine adds this check to every rule. No rule can leave it out.
    5. For each field, the first bound rule without reasons grants the field (engine.rego#L269-L306).
    6. The engine allows the request only if it allows every data field.

    Service binding is necessary because a field key is unique only within one schema. Query.ingeschrevenPersoon is in both bri and brp. If the binding is absent, a rule for one service grants the same key on the other service (F-90). A test requires every rule to name its services (engine_test.rego#L497-L501).

    The world is closed. If no rule covers a field, the engine denies the field with NO_APPLICABLE_RULE. No separate catalog exists: the rule is the catalog. If the engine cannot make a decision for a field, it refuses the field as RULE_NOT_EVALUABLE. The request then fails as a configuration error (engine.rego#L18-L23). The engine never leaves a field out of the decision.

    Constraints inside the query¶

    Field coverage answers "which fields". Two more checks answer "whose records" and "which part of the records". Both checks read the arguments of the query. So the selectors must be inside the query, where the PDP can see them. The two checks work as follows:

    • The subject check. Under consent, the query names the citizen with a placeholder: consent:identity for a BSN API, consent:pseudonym for a source-pseudonym API (lib.rego#L43-L53). Each rule lists the placeholders that it accepts. DVT0001 and LVG0001 accept only consent:identity. The PDP denies three cases with CONSTRAINT_MISMATCH: a literal value, another placeholder, and a placeholder without a verified proof (dvt0001.rego#L72-L80).

      The PDP does not check who the subject is. It checks that the subject comes from the proof (REQ-79, F-77).

    • The year check. Every requested tax year (belastingjaren) needs a consented bd:ib:<year> scope. If a query has no year filter, it fails too, because the source then returns every year (dvt0001.rego#L82-L96). An argument that comes from a schema default counts as missing.

    The source returns only the fields that the query selects (REQ-08).

    Consent verification in policy¶

    The policy verifies the consent proof itself (ADR-0032, consent.rego). The request mapper has no part in this verification. The policy ignores a pip.consent in the input. The PDP decides only on a consent for which it established the origin, the binding, and the status at evaluation time itself (REQ-68).

    For each evaluation, the policy does three steps in this order:

    1. It verifies the ES256 signature against the JWKS of the register. It caches the JWKS for 300 seconds and fetches the JWKS again on an unknown kid.
    2. It verifies the claims, with 30 seconds of clock skew.
    3. Only then does it call the register for the status of the consent_id. This call goes over FSC, with no cache and a 2-second timeout.

    Each failure maps to its own reason code (consent.rego#L174-L186):

    Code Cause
    CONSENT_CONTEXT_INVALID Two tokens. A wrong type, issuer, or audience. A missing claim or no encrypted_subject. A valid_until that is not equal to exp
    CONSENT_SIGNATURE_INVALID The token is no JWT, the algorithm is other than ES256, the key is unknown, or the signature does not verify
    CONSENT_KEYS_UNAVAILABLE The policy cannot fetch the JWKS
    CONSENT_TOKEN_EXPIRED The time is more than 30 seconds after exp
    CONSENT_STATUS_UNAVAILABLE The status lookup failed or timed out
    CONSENT_NOT_FOUND The register does not know the consent
    CONSENT_WITHDRAWN The status is REVOKED
    CONSENT_EXPIRED The time is after valid_until, within the clock skew
    CONSENT_ACTOR_MISMATCH The consent names a party other than the represented party of the call

    The consent binds the represented party. On a delegated call, this party is the FSC delegator. On other calls, it is the calling peer (lib.rego#L55-L72). The integrator gets no mandate from the consent (REQ-106, ADR-0034).

    The policy fetches the status during evaluation. As a result, the input, the policy, and the data do not reproduce the decision. The engine copies the resolved consent into its response for the console decision log (engine.rego#L25-L29). The ADL does not contain this copy (F-72). For the proof, the status interface, and the freshness rules, see Consent.

    Query mapping (FTV GraphQL profile)¶

    The GraphQL query of the consumer is the authorization object. The PEP sends the raw body. The request mapper inside the PDP turns the body into the field list of the FTV GraphQL profile for AuthZEN (ftv-graphql/0.1). The mapper is a separate Go module, services/ftv-graphql-mapper, with a thin OpenFTV adapter (ADR-0013).

    The mapper applies four rules:

    • It parses the body. It gives each field its parent type from the bundled schema of the FSC service of the request. It gives each field its arguments as the source executes them.
    • It accepts only a query. A mutation or a subscription gives OPERATION_NOT_SUPPORTED (mapper.go#L194).
    • It enforces limits: body 1 MiB, nesting depth 64, 100 fragment definitions, and selection depth 64. Further limits are 1000 field records, 100 aliased selections, and 1 second of validation (mapper.go#L252-L268).
    • It never accepts persistedQuery.

    If the mapper cannot build a complete field list, it marks the request Unverifiable with a code and a subcode (mapper.go#L27-L43). The engine then denies the whole request (REQ-17). The mapper uses these codes and subcodes:

    Code Subcodes
    COVERAGE_UNVERIFIABLE UNSUPPORTED_TRANSPORT, INVALID_BODY, PARSE_ERROR, INVALID_QUERY, NO_OPERATION, OPERATION_NOT_FOUND, OPERATION_AMBIGUOUS, VARIABLE_ERROR, LIMIT_EXCEEDED
    OPERATION_NOT_SUPPORTED —
    CONFIG_ERROR SCHEMA_UNAVAILABLE

    Three controls keep the judged request equal to the executed request:

    • Schema pins: the policy bundle pins the digest of the schema of each service in graphql_schemas.rego. If a schema is not pinned, the PDP denies with CONFIG_ERROR SCHEMA_MISMATCH (engine.rego#L129-L141).
    • Drift check: a CI job compares the bundled schemas with the schemas that the sources run (check-schema-drift.sh).
    • Transport subset at the source: the source gateway accepts only POST with a JSON body on one path. It accepts no query string, no Upgrade, and no Content-Encoding (transport.go#L9-L13). A request that the PDP never judged cannot run.

    For future sources, how the PDP models fields, recursion, and arguments is an open question (Q-14).

    Reason codes: two layers¶

    A denial carries a machine-readable reason in two layers (REQ-06). The consumer gets a coarse code. The administrator of the source gets the detail per field. The consumer code never shows which field the PDP denied, whether a field exists, or which check failed. Otherwise the consumer can map the schema by trying names. The two layers differ in audience, route, and codes:

    Layer Who sees it Where it goes Codes
    Consumer code (graphql.client) Consumer, ADL reason → reason_user.en in the AuthZEN answer. The ADL stores it FIELD_NOT_PERMITTED, ACCESS_DENIED, COVERAGE_UNVERIFIABLE <subcode>, OPERATION_NOT_SUPPORTED, NO_DATA_FIELDS
    Administrator codes (graphql.admin) Administrator of the source OPA console decision log only (observability) Request code, plus per denied field: the bound rules, their reasons in order, and the field code

    Each administrator request code maps to one consumer code (engine.rego#L95-L118, authz.rego#L42-L51):

    Administrator request code Consumer code
    Fields denied by rules (FIELD_NOT_PERMITTED) FIELD_NOT_PERMITTED
    COVERAGE_UNVERIFIABLE INVALID_QUERY FIELD_NOT_PERMITTED
    COVERAGE_UNVERIFIABLE with another subcode COVERAGE_UNVERIFIABLE <subcode>
    OPERATION_NOT_SUPPORTED, NO_DATA_FIELDS the same code
    PIP_UNAVAILABLE (the consent register, its keys, or the admission register did not answer) ACCESS_DENIED
    CONFIG_ERROR (MAPPER_OUTPUT_MISSING, SCHEMA_MISMATCH, SCHEMA_UNAVAILABLE, RULE_NOT_EVALUABLE) ACCESS_DENIED

    To the consumer, a fault at the source looks like a normal denial. For one field, a rule can give several reasons. The rule reports the first reason in a fixed order (engine.rego#L321-L344). The order is the token, then the state of the consent, then the question, then the caller. As a result, if the consent is revoked and the year check also fails, the code is CONSENT_WITHDRAWN.

    Demo v0.9.0 has two limits for reason codes:

    • The FSC Inway loses the reason. It reads reasonUser, but the PDP sends reason_user. Upstream has a fix that was not released at the time of demo v0.9.0 (ftv-graphql-profile.md#L93-L96).
    • The consumer backend shows the citizen only FIELD_NOT_PERMITTED, with an offer to consent again. Every other code becomes UNAVAILABLE (denial.go).

    The ADL is the audit source (ADR-0036). It holds only the consumer code. As a result, a supervisor can reconstruct from the ADL only what the consumer can know (F-72). For the full list of deny paths per scenario, see the runtime view, for example DvTP query.

    Admission and contract acceptance¶

    Admission to the system is data in a register. The decision policy holds no admissions (REQ-61). The FSC Manager of the provider sends every contract proposal to the PDP. The contract policy (autosign.rego) reads the admission register and runs eight checks. The first check that fails names the refusal (ADR-0015, autosign.rego#L165-L175). The policy runs the checks in this order:

    # Code Refuses when
    1 NOT_AN_AUTOSIGN_REQUEST The input is not a well-formed autosign request
    2 GRANT_TYPE_NOT_ALLOWED The grants are not all type 2 (service connection) or all type 3 (delegated service connection)
    3 NO_COUNTERPARTY The contract has no party other than the provider itself
    4 ADMISSION_REGISTER_UNAVAILABLE The PIP pull supplied no register
    5 PARTY_NOT_IN_REGISTRY A party is not in the register
    6 PARTY_NOT_ACTIVE A party is suspended
    7 SOURCE_NOT_ALLOWED The party is not admitted for this source peer
    8 DELEGATION_NOT_REGISTERED A delegated grant has no registered integration

    A missing register and an empty register are different (autosign.rego#L51-L53). An empty register is available data that admits nobody. After a refusal, the contract stays proposed, so the party can submit it again (REQ-63).

    The contract question and the request question are separate rule sets (REQ-62). A contract decides who can connect at all. A request decides which field the party can read at request time. The two rule sets share no rules and no reason codes. They do share one availability object: one broken module stops both (F-52).

    Four points are open:

    • A suspended consumer keeps its existing contract. It can still send queries, also with a valid consent (REQ-110, Q-53).
    • No component logs changes to admissions, mandates, and activations (REQ-123).
    • The autosign input of the Manager carries only peer IDs and grant types. As a result, the policy judges only the parties of a contract. It has no input about the content of the contract (F-56).
    • The task to run the admission register is assigned to the management organization (Q-22).

    For the scenario, see Admission and activation.

    Data scope: demand side and supply side¶

    What a consumer can request depends on two sides (F-74):

    • Supply side: the source publishes what it offers. GBO validates and activates this description (REQ-64, Source onboarding). The EUDI and ASI routes work this way.
    • Demand side: for DvTP, a statutory service catalog (dienstencatalogus) sets the legal ceiling of what a consumer can request, per use case. The sector need defines this catalog.

    What is technically allowed is the intersection of both sides. No text in the GO, the PSA, or the FR-DvTP names that intersection. In demo v0.9.0, the DvTP scopes are spread over the rules, the portal, and the field coverage. The proposal is one DvTP catalog as the single source for scopes, fields, and portal text. The proposal also adds an intersection check at activation (REQ-121, #382).

    Traceability¶

    • Requirements: REQ-04, REQ-06, REQ-08, REQ-17, REQ-18, REQ-42, REQ-44, REQ-45, REQ-48, REQ-61, REQ-62, REQ-63, REQ-64, REQ-68, REQ-74, REQ-79, REQ-90, REQ-97, REQ-106, REQ-110, REQ-121, REQ-123
    • Findings: F-35 (resolved in demo), F-52 (open), F-56 (closed), F-70 (open), F-72 (open), F-74 (open), F-77 (open), F-83 (open), F-90 (resolved in demo)

    Consent¶

    In DvTP, the consent of the citizen is the legal basis for delivery of source data to a private consumer (afnemer). A consent proof carries the consent to the source, and the PDP of the source verifies that proof on every request. A consent has a lifecycle of validity, revocation, and repeated use. The consent model realizes capability S01 for the consent register (toestemmingsregister) and capability S02 for the consent portal (toestemmingsportaal).

    The main decision is ADR-0032. It defines the consent proof in five points:

    • The register signs the proof.
    • The proof carries a value per source.
    • The consumer can name the citizen only with a placeholder.
    • The status stays online over FSC.
    • The policy verifies the proof.

    For the scenarios, see the runtime view: DvTP consent, DvTP query, and DvTP citizen access.

    Roles¶

    Five roles take part in consent:

    Role Component in the demo Does
    Consent portal (S02) toestemmingsportaal-frontend, consent portal backend Shows the request, logs the citizen in, makes the values per source at BSNk, and lets the citizen view and revoke consents
    Consent register (S01) consent-register Stores the consent record, signs the proof, and answers the status over FSC
    Consumer dienstverlener-backend Starts the request, receives the proof, and sends it unchanged with every query
    PDP of the source OpenFTV PDP, consent.rego Verifies the proof and gets the status at every request
    Source gateway bron-sidecar After the allow, decrypts its own value from the proof

    It is an open question whether the register and the portal backend are one system (Q-49). For the requirements on the roles, see Consent roles.

    Lifecycle¶

    stateDiagram-v2 [*] --> Active: citizen gives consent<br/>register signs the proof Active --> Active: consumer queries<br/>(repeated use) Active --> Revoked: citizen revokes Active --> Expired: valid_until passes Revoked --> [*] Expired --> [*] classDef active fill:#DCFCE7,stroke:#16A34A,color:#0F172A classDef stop fill:#FEDCD8,stroke:#E28F80,color:#1E293B class Active active class Revoked,Expired stop

    The register stores the status ACTIVE or REVOKED. The status Expired follows from valid_until. The citizen overview shows Active, Expired, and Revoked. Demo v0.9.0 does not build a "retrieved" status. Two points are open: when a consent counts as retrieved, and how the register learns this (Q-42). The FR-DvTP texts name the statuses with different words (F-97).

    A consent is bound to one consumer, one service, and named data sets (REQ-12). It covers a whole data set. Within a set, the citizen does not pick fields (REQ-10). The portal shows only the data sets that the consumer asks for. It refuses a data set that it cannot describe. For the record model, see consent register.

    The consent proof¶

    When the citizen gives consent, the consent register signs a JWT with these parts (consent_token.go#L130-L152):

    Part Content
    Header alg=ES256, typ=gbo-consent+jwt, kid. The public keys are in the JWKS of the register
    consent_id, jti The consent and a unique token ID
    scopes, scope_entries The data sets, per source
    dienstverlener_oin The represented party. In the demo, this field holds the FSC Peer ID (Q-68)
    valid_until, exp The end of the validity. The two values are equal
    iss, aud, iat, nbf Issuer, audience (default gbo:dvtp:pdp), and times
    encrypted_subject For each source OIN: a pseudonym (VP) and, only for a source on the BSN authorization list, an identity (VI). Each value has its key_set_version

    The proof holds no BSN and no PI (REQ-20). Only the source that a value in encrypted_subject was made for can read that value (REQ-80). The register refuses a proof without a pseudonym for every party (consent_token.go#L45-L64). The PDP denies such a proof too, with CONSENT_CONTEXT_INVALID. For how the values are made, see Pseudonymization.

    The portal returns the proof to the consumer in the URL fragment of the return redirect. The consumer frontend removes the proof from the visible URL at once (consent-flow.md#L130-L133). The question of what the return redirect gives back is partly answered (Q-44).

    The consumer sends the proof unchanged in X-GBO-Consent-Token (AV-05). In its query, the consumer names the citizen only with a placeholder: consent:identity for a BSN API, consent:pseudonym for a source-pseudonym API (REQ-79). The consumer can read consent_id and scopes from the proof. It cannot read who the citizen is (F-76).

    The integrator is not in the proof¶

    An integrator calls the source for a consumer under FSC delegation (ADR-0034). The proof binds only the represented party, which is the consumer. The integrator needs its own mandate for each consumer and rule in the admission register (REQ-106). If this mandate is absent, the PDP denies with INTEGRATOR_NOT_REGISTERED.

    It is an open question whether the proof must also bind the integrator (Q-46). The working assumption is that it does not. If the integrator is in the proof, a change of integrator makes all running consents unusable. If the integrator is not in the proof, every registered integrator of that consumer can use the proof.

    Bearer token¶

    The proof is a bearer token. The actor binding stops use by another consumer. It does not stop replay by the same consumer (consent-flow.md#L268-L273). Production needs a shorter validity and proof-of-possession binding to the FSC identity (Risks).

    The location and the rotation of the signing key are open (Q-55). If the register uses a persistent store, it needs a fixed signing key (CONSENT_SIGNING_KEY_PATH). Then proofs stay valid after a restart (main.go#L84-L86).

    Verification and status¶

    The PDP of the source decides only on a consent that it checked itself (REQ-68). It establishes the origin, the binding, and the status at evaluation time. The policy does this work. The request mapper has no part in it (consent.rego). The policy verifies the proof and gets the status in this sequence:

    sequenceDiagram box rgb(220,252,231) GBO Basis participant IN as Source Inway (PEP) participant PDP as PDP policy (consent.rego) participant OUT as PDP Outway participant CRIN as Register Inway end box rgb(254,220,216) DvTP participant CR as Consent register end IN->>PDP: AuthZEN evaluation with X-GBO-Consent-Token opt JWKS not cached, older than 300 s, or unknown kid PDP->>CR: GET /.well-known/jwks.json end Note over PDP: verify ES256 signature,<br/>then claims (30 s skew) PDP->>OUT: GET /consent-status/consents/{id}/status<br/>(no cache, 2 s timeout) OUT->>CRIN: FSC (mTLS + access token) CRIN->>CR: status listener (port 4012) CR-->>PDP: ACTIVE, REVOKED or 404 Note over PDP: actor binding, scope,<br/>placeholder, years, fields PDP-->>IN: allow or deny

    The policy handles keys, claims, and status as follows:

    • Keys: the policy gets the JWKS directly from the register. It caches the JWKS for 300 seconds and fetches it again on an unknown kid, so a new key works at once. No stale-key fallback exists, because the register that serves the keys also answers the status (consent.rego#L70-L90).
    • Claims: the policy verifies type, issuer, audience, required claims, nbf, iat, and valid_until == exp, with 30 seconds of clock skew. The policy reads the claims only after the signature verifies, so a forged token never reaches the register (consent.rego#L169-L186).
    • Status: the policy gets the status for each evaluation, with no cache, a 2-second timeout, and raise_error: false. The call carries traceparent and Fsc-Transaction-Id (consent.rego#L190-L200). It goes over FSC, from the Outway of the PDP (peer …0800) to the Inway of the register (peer …0700, FSC service consent-status).

    The register serves the status on its own listener. This listener serves nothing else (status.go#L13-L26). A lookup without an FSC peer gets 401. The register logs each lookup as a processing, with the calling peer as processor (REQ-76).

    The FSC Manager of the register signs a contract only for the peer of the PDP. Still, any connected peer can get the status of a consent if it holds the consent ID. Demo v0.9.0 does not restrict lookups to the PDP of the source that the consent is for.

    Each failure has its own reason code. For the table of codes, see Authorization.

    Freshness is asymmetric on purpose¶

    The legal basis travels as a proof, and the status stays online (F-61). Each part has its own freshness:

    What Freshness Why
    Proof content (scopes, party, validity) Fixed at consent, verified locally The register signed it. The PDP needs no lookup for it
    Verification keys Up to 300 seconds old Keys change rarely. An unknown kid causes a fetch at once
    Status Live at every request A revocation must deny the next request (REQ-14)

    If the status is unknown, the PDP denies. So the register is a dependency of every DvTP request (REQ-75). The values for propagation time, availability, and latency are open (Q-47). The question of who is authoritative for revocation and expiry is answered: the register, with the status online and fail closed (Q-05).

    The status answer is not in the PDP input. As a result, the input, the policy, and the data do not reproduce a decision. The ADL does not hold the answer (F-72).

    Validity¶

    A consent has a finite validity. After the validity ends, the PDP denies (REQ-19). Three rules set the validity:

    • The register sets valid_until at creation, and the proof has exp = valid_until.
    • The PDP checks both values. Within 30 seconds after valid_until, it denies with CONSENT_EXPIRED. After that, the token check denies first, with CONSENT_TOKEN_EXPIRED.
    • In the demo, the consumer chooses the period with validity_seconds. The default is one year, with no upper bound (main.go#L48-L51, main.go#L421-L424). The citizen cannot change the period (F-11, #380).

    Since November 2, 2026, the question of who sets the validity period is open again (Q-13). Under FR-11, the default can come from the service catalog, and the citizen can adjust it within bounds. It is a policy and UX choice whether the citizen must be able to do this. It is also open whether the validity can differ per source within one consent (Q-76). The working assumption is one validity per consent.

    Revocation¶

    The citizen views and revokes consents in the portal (REQ-38). Before it revokes a consent, the portal backend derives the reference of the citizen. It then checks that the consent belongs to that citizen (portal.go#L268-L293, REQ-40). Viewing and revoking need no BSNk call.

    The register sets the status to REVOKED and keeps the record. It writes the processing record in the same transaction (main.go#L585-L596). For the next request on that proof, the status is REVOKED, and the PDP denies with CONSENT_WITHDRAWN (REQ-14). Another active consent of the same citizen cannot take its place, because the PDP checks only the consent_id from the signed proof.

    Three points on revocation are open:

    • Revocation of a valid consent only (REQ-109).
    • Whether the register records the moment of revocation (Q-48).
    • A pointer to the rights of the citizen at the consumer after revocation (REQ-120).

    Repeated use, not single use¶

    Within its validity, a consumer can use a consent again (REQ-19). The design removed single use (Q-04, answered, after FR-11). The demo has no reuse check. The status machine of SL-01b waits for the "retrieved" status (Q-42).

    The LVG pilot uses repeated use. The Installatie Register keeps the proof. It sends a new request at every installer access, under one consent. Revocation stops this use (lvg-ir.md#L59-L61).

    The proof freezes at consent¶

    BSNk transforms only while the citizen is logged in (BSNK-04). So all values in the proof are made at consent time. Parties, key versions, BSN authorization, and proof form are fixed for the whole validity period (F-78). This has four consequences:

    • A source that joins later needs a new consent.
    • If a source gets a new key version, it keeps its old keys while proofs for the old version are valid (AV-09).
    • A source that joins the BSN authorization list later has only a pseudonym in older consents.
    • A new proof form makes every outstanding proof fail with CONSENT_CONTEXT_INVALID. The proof has no version field.

    It is an open question what counts as a change of a consent (Q-77). When consent is given, the register must know the OIN, the key version, and the BSN authorization of each source (REQ-82).

    Consent in other routes¶

    DvTP consent is a registered, revocable legal basis. Approval in the wallet (EUDI) and login at the ASI authorization server are a different thing. They are the choice of the citizen for each presentation or each request. Neither is a legal basis, and neither replaces the other (F-83, Authorization).

    What travels where¶

    Each tag names a kind of data that a hop carries. The runtime view uses the same tags. The tags are in order of sensitivity:

    Tag Meaning Sensitivity Where
    query and variables GraphQL query and variables. They select data sets and carry no identity data under consent low Every transport hop
    OIN / Peer ID Organization identifier of the consumer low FSC token, PDP input, decision logs
    scope Data-set code, for example bd:ib:2025 low Every DvTP and EUDI hop
    FSC token Certificate-bound JWT of the FSC Manager of the provider. It carries no grant properties medium (transport authentication) Outway, Inway, PDP. The source gateway reads only the caller, for its logbook
    consent_id Handle to the consent record medium (linkable to the citizen through the register) Inside the proof. Alone, only in the status lookup and the citizen UI
    consent proof Signed (ES256), audience-bound JWT with consent_id, encrypted_subject, scopes, dienstverlener_oin, and valid_until medium-high (carries the values per source and the legal basis) Consumer → FSC → PDP → source gateway, in X-GBO-Consent-Token. Never in observer or history payloads
    VI (encrypted identity) Value that BSNk makes for one party and key version. That party decrypts it to the BSN. Only for a party on the BSN authorization list high at the recipient, unreadable for others (readable in the demo: the mock does not encrypt) Only inside the proof. The source gateway takes its own value after the allow
    VP (encrypted pseudonym) Value that BSNk makes for one party and key version. That party decrypts it to its own pseudonym of the citizen. Every party gets one medium at the recipient, unreadable for others (readable in the demo) Only inside the proof. Demo v0.9.0 does not build a VP for the consumer (#478)
    placeholder consent:identity or consent:pseudonym in the place of the subject none (identifies nobody) Consumer → FSC → PDP → source gateway, which replaces it
    PI / PP Polymorphic identity and pseudonym of BSNk. Only the requester can use them medium (only BSNk can transform them) Portal backend. Stored in the register under subject_ref (route D)
    subject_ref HMAC of the BSN with the secret key of the portal medium (computable from a BSN with the key) Portal backend, register
    BSN Plain citizen service number high (personal data) DvTP: the portal backend at login, and the source after the allow. EUDI and ASI: through the flow, and in both PDP decision logs (ADR-0043)

    Open points¶

    Nine points on consent are open:

    • Purpose binding in the proof (Q-69).
    • Proof of what the citizen saw at consent (Q-51, REQ-107, REQ-117).
    • Mandatory minimal data sets (Q-45).
    • Consent by an authorized representative (Q-73, REQ-118).
    • Recording of a refusal (Q-43).
    • Recording of the first use of a consent, which the FR-22 usage status needs (F-19).
    • Durability and recovery of the register storage (Q-54).
    • What the management organization records or delivers for the consent process (Q-62).
    • Security requirements for the portal UI inside MijnOverheid, and what MijnOverheid must deliver or allow (Q-59, Q-61).

    Pseudonymization¶

    Private consumers must not process the BSN (P-04). In DvTP, they still request data about one citizen from government sources. For this, GBO uses the BSNk PP polymorphic pseudonym scheme. GBO calls BSNk only at consent time (ADR-0005). In the consent route, the consumer holds no identifier of the citizen: no BSN and no pseudonym (REQ-20). After the PDP allows the request, only the source turns its own value back into the BSN (ADR-0033).

    Pseudonymization realizes capability S03. For the BSNk rules that shape this design, see BSNk preconditions. For the consent proof that carries the values, see Consent.

    Identifiers¶

    Each identifier of the citizen or the consent has its own maker and holder:

    Identifier What it is Made by Held by
    BSN The citizen service number DigiD login, or PID disclosure (EUDI, ASI) The portal backend during the login. The source, inside its own boundary
    PI, PP Polymorphic identity and polymorphic pseudonym. Only the requester can get them transformed (BSNK-03) BSNk Activate, once per citizen The portal backend. The register stores them under subject_ref (REQ-69)
    VI (encrypted identity) A value for one recipient OIN and key version. It decrypts to the BSN. It exists only for a recipient on the BSN authorization list (BSNK-06) BSNk Transform, at consent Inside the consent proof, encrypted_subject[<OIN>].identity
    VP (encrypted pseudonym) A value for one recipient OIN and key version. It decrypts to the own pseudonym of that recipient for the citizen. Every recipient gets one BSNk Transform, at consent Inside the consent proof, encrypted_subject[<OIN>].pseudonym
    Placeholder consent:identity or consent:pseudonym: the name of the subject in a consent-based query Fixed values (lib.rego#L43-L53) The consumer query and the PDP input. The source gateway replaces it
    subject_ref HMAC of the BSN with the secret, versioned key of the portal Portal backend (subjectref.go#L38-L42) Portal backend and register: the key to the consents of the citizen
    consent_id The consent record Consent register (toestemmingsregister) Consumer: its only handle on "this person"

    PI and PP belong to the portal. VI and VP belong to their recipient. No other party can read them. In the demo, every party can read them because the mock does not encrypt. For more information, see Demo mock and production BSNk.

    Where each identifier lives¶
