    Values made at consent time¶

    BSNk transforms values only while the citizen is logged in (BSNK-04). A query comes later. As a result, the portal makes every value that a source needs while the citizen gives consent (portal.go#L119-L192). The portal does these steps:

    1. It derives subject_ref from the BSN.
    2. It looks up PI and PP under subject_ref in the register. At the first consent of this citizen, it activates the BSN once at BSNk and stores PI and PP (portal.go#L296-L314).
    3. It reads the BSN authorization list from a copy. The copy is at most BSN_AUTHORISATION_LIST_MAX_AGE old (default 1 hour).
    4. It transforms PP to a VP for every source. It transforms PI to a VI for every source on the list (portal.go#L197-L224). Each BSNk request names at most four parties (BSNK-05, bsnk.go#L102-L115).
    5. It sends the values to the register. The register signs them into the proof and does not store them.

    For each source, the portal must know the OIN, the key version, and the BSN authorization (REQ-82). In the demo, this is configuration: CONSENT_SOURCES=<OIN>@<key set version> (docker-compose.yml#L1005). If no source is configured, the portal gives no consent. A service catalogue that carries these facts is not built (#382).

    The portal makes all values at consent, so the proof freezes. For more information, see Consent (F-78).

    Citizen recognition: route D¶

    To show and revoke the consents of a citizen without a BSN, the consent facility (toestemmingsvoorziening) needs a stable key. A stored PI or PP is not a stable key, because BSNk gives other values at every activation. The proposed solution is route D (ADR-0040, proposed, route D). Route D works as follows:

    • The service recognizes the citizen by an HMAC of the BSN, with a secret, versioned key. Every record keeps the key version.
    • The service activates once and stores PI and PP under that reference.
    • To show or revoke consents, the service does not call BSNk.

    The register stores PI and PP, but no BSN and no per-party value (REQ-69, REQ-23). This is an intentional deviation from FR-35, criterion 1 (F-98). For the other routes, see BSNk preconditions.

    Route D has these open points:

    • Are the register and the portal backend one BSNk participant (Q-49)? In the demo, the backend activates and the register stores.
    • A changed HMAC key gives every citizen a different reference. Then the service does not show older consents. Migration is not built (Q-56).
    • The protection of the stored PI and PP is open (Q-57). Retention is also open (Q-63).

    Where the boundary is enforced¶

    The BSN is in three places only. All three places are inside the government:

    1. Portal backend, at login: the backend derives subject_ref. At the first consent, it sends the BSN to BSNk. After that step, no component holds a BSN, because the draft consent has no field for one (portal.go#L116-L118). It is open how the backend inside MijnOverheid gets the verified identity (Q-50).
    2. BSNk, at activation: BSNk records every activation in its inspection register, the Inzageregister (BSNK-10).
    3. The source, after the allow: the source gateway takes the value for its own OIN from the proof. The decryption component of the source reads the value with the keys of the source. The gateway accepts the result only if the value names the OIN of the source as recipient (substitution.go#L213-L251, REQ-80). Then the gateway replaces the placeholder. BSNk is not in the query path (REQ-21).

    The register never gets a BSN, not even for a short time (REQ-23). The consumer never gets a BSN in the proof or in the response.

    Like the PDP, the gateway acts on the evidence. If the request carries a consent token, the gateway takes the subject from the token. If the request has no consent token, the gateway passes it through unchanged (PID regime). The gateway reads no grant property. The value for the requested form can be missing, for example no VI for a source that is not on the list. In that case, the gateway does not forward the request.

    Network isolation is the control¶

    The gateway does not verify the proof again (substitution.go#L105-L107). A second check adds nothing, because a consumer holds real proofs. The rule "after the decision" holds only while the Inway is the only component that reaches the gateway (REQ-81, F-79).

    In the demo, the gateways publish no port. They are on two networks only:

    • source-gateways, shared with the source Inways.
    • sources, shared with the source services, the decryption component, and the logbooks (docker-compose.yml#L829-L836).

    No consumer is on either network. Outside Docker Compose, this isolation needs a Kubernetes NetworkPolicy or an equivalent control. The Helm chart in demo v0.9.0 has no NetworkPolicy. A nonce that binds a value to one consent, as a second line, is not built. For the zones, see Deployment.

    Subject binding¶

    Under a consent, the PDP does not compare identifiers. The query names the subject with a placeholder. The source can fill in only the subject from the proof (REQ-79, F-77). For the rule, see Authorization. Subject binding has these consequences:

    • No policy at the PDP can depend on who the citizen is.
    • One request names one subject. A question about two persons does not fit. This needs a design decision.
    • Substitution works only on variables. If the query text holds a literal placeholder, the placeholder passes the PDP. The gateway does not replace it, and the query finds nobody.
    • The PDP input and the decision logs have no identifier. They do hold the proof with the encrypted values.

    The consumer has no identifier¶

    The consumer reads only consent_id and scopes from the proof (F-76). This goes further than the "BSN-free" rule of P-04, because the consumer is free of all identifiers. This has three effects:

    • Logging: the consumer logbook names the data subject by the consent ID, with subject type consent-id (logbook.go#L20-L22). In the logbook, one citizen with two consents is two data subjects. It is open whether this fits LDV (Q-27).
    • Access requests: a citizen can ask the consumer what it processed. The consumer can find the citizen only through the consents of the citizen.
    • Recognition: through GBO, the consumer cannot tell that two consents are from the same person. This is data minimization, and a design choice.

    With its own VP, the consumer has a pseudonym to log under. This option is in the design and not built (#478, Q-01). A source API that answers on a pseudonym is also not built. No demo rule accepts consent:pseudonym (#474).

    Exception: the BSN in the EUDI and ASI routes¶

    The EUDI adapter and the ASIP put the plain BSN from the PID or the token into the query variables. As a result, the BSN is in the PDP input and in both decision logs: the ADL and the console log (source_metadata.go#L273, source.go#L94). The PDP does not call BSNk. This is a known violation of REQ-60. The demo accepts it until #368 decides between masking and "transform first" (CHANGELOG).

    The proposed decision keeps identifiers out of the PDP input and uses masking only as a second line (ADR-0043, proposed). Earlier, masking in the policy engine had no effect (F-54). LDV records never hold a BSN, because the logbook refuses one (Logging).

    Demo mock and production BSNk¶

    The demo uses bsnk-mock (README). The mock follows the BSNk interface (/v2/activate, /v2/transform, /v2/bsn-authorisation-list, and more), but as JSON instead of SOAP. The mock enforces these rules:

    • Only the requester can use the PI.
    • The BSN authorization list applies.
    • A request names at most four parties.
    • The mock reads values per key version.

    The mock and production BSNk differ in these properties:

    Property Demo Production
    Encryption None: any party that holds a PI or VI can read the BSN Encrypted values, unlinkable between parties
    Values Stable by default. Random with RANDOMIZE_VALUES=true, as real BSNk Different at every request
    Interface JSON over HTTP SOAP with PKIoverheid (BSNK-11)
    Who can activate Not checked: the mock takes the requester from the request Only a recognized participant (BSNK-01, F-75, Q-26)
    Activation input The BSN. The mock does not check it against a population register The BSN and check data (BSNK-02)
    Recipient keys Demo keys in the gateway image Per recipient through an Access Service or Key Requester (BSNK-09, #467)
    Key versions The mock accepts any key set version A value belongs to one key version. The source keeps older keys while proofs for them are valid (BSNK-08, AV-09)
    Decryption component One, shared by the three demo sources, which also share one OIN One per source, each with its own OIN (BSNK-07)

    The same image, started with DECRYPTION_COMPONENT_ONLY=true, is the decryption component of the sources (docker-compose.yml#L773-L786). The mock does not encrypt and the sources share one OIN. As a result, the demo does not show unlinkability between parties. For the certificates and keys per party at onboarding, see BSNk preconditions.

    Traceability¶

    • Requirements: REQ-20, REQ-21, REQ-23, REQ-60, REQ-69, REQ-79, REQ-80, REQ-81, REQ-82, AV-09, BSNK-01, BSNK-02, BSNK-03, BSNK-04, BSNK-05, BSNK-06, BSNK-07, BSNK-08, BSNK-09, BSNK-10, BSNK-11
    • Findings: F-30 (resolved in demo), F-54 (open), F-75 (open), F-76 (open), F-77 (open), F-78 (open), F-79 (open), F-98 (open)
    • Open questions: Q-01 (partly answered), Q-26 (open), Q-27 (open), Q-49 (open), Q-50 (open), Q-56 (open), Q-57 (open), Q-63 (open)
    • Demo increments: SL-02 (done), SL-22 (done), SL-29 (done), SL-51 (done)

    Source onboarding¶

    A GBO component must know, for each source, which data service to call, with which query, and what to do with the answer. That knowledge comes from the source itself, and GBO takes a source into use in a fixed set of steps. The decisions are ADR-0016 (mechanism), ADR-0017 (mapping profile for attestations), and ADR-0039 (attributes for the ASIP). For the requirements, see Source metadata and activation. For the components, see the building block view. For the step-by-step flow, see Admission and activation.

    The behavior on this page is the behavior of gbo-demo v0.9.0 (docs/source-onboarding.md, docs/source-metadata-cache.md).

    Why the source owns its description¶

    The bronhouder keeps control of its data (P-10). It can add services through its source-specific GBO configuration (S07). Central GBO facilities read the part of this configuration that they need. They read it in machine-readable form, validated and versioned (S10).

    As a result, a GBO component takes the service description of a source only from what the source publishes itself (REQ-64, F-57):

    • The component does not keep the description, add to it, or carry it per source in code.
    • A new service or attestation type needs no code change in GBO.
    • The source does not publish its GraphQL schema. It publishes the queries and mappings that it takes responsibility for.

    Before this mechanism, every new source, attestation type, or tax year was a change in GBO code or in a GBO catalog file. With this mechanism, the adapter parameters come from the source (Q-19). In GO terms, the document is the service catalog (dienstencatalogus) that the bronhouder manages. The validation rules of the reconciler are the common profile.

    The mechanism (publish, validate, activate, roll back) is a GBO design decision. The document format gbo-source-metadata-v1 is the proposal of the demo for the open PSA S10 decision. It is not a final interface agreement.

    Three inputs together describe a source. Each input has a different owner:

    Item Owner Where
    source_id, transport, metadata location, FSC Peer ID GBO operator source configuration file (sources/configured/<source_id>.yaml)
    Legal OIN, organization name, issuer name and logo bronhouder, through its certificate certificate set under the key source_id (Identity and trust)
    Access to the metadata and data services bronhouder and GBO, by agreement FSC contracts and grant hashes
    Data service, query, parameters, offers, display, claims, attributes bronhouder the source document at /.well-known/gbo
    Shape of an ASI attribute value (value_schema) GBO, until the EU catalog of attributes exists schemas/asi-attributes.json
    SD-JWT VC Type Metadata GBO generates it from the document source registry
    Candidates, states, releases, active pointer GBO source registry (PostgreSQL)

    Lifecycle¶

    flowchart LR A[1 Configure<br/>source file] --> B[2 Discover<br/>FSC contracts] B --> C[3 Fetch or read<br/>the document] C --> D[4 Validate] D --> E[5 Candidate<br/>rollout_required] E --> F[6 Promote] F --> G[7 Immutable<br/>release] G --> H[8 Active<br/>pointer] H --> I[9 Runtime<br/>reload] D -- invalid --> X[source stale<br/>or blocked] %% GBO diagram palette: the same colors as the Globaal Ontwerp classDef basis fill:#DCFCE7,stroke:#16A34A,color:#0F172A classDef dvtp fill:#FEDCD8,stroke:#E28F80,color:#1E293B classDef eudi fill:#FFEDD5,stroke:#EA580C,color:#0F172A classDef source fill:#DDEBF7,stroke:#6F94B8,color:#1E293B classDef ext fill:#F1EFE8,stroke:#5F5E5A,color:#444441 classDef store fill:#EDE9FE,stroke:#7C3AED,color:#1E1B4B classDef mock fill:#F3F4F6,stroke:#9CA3AF,color:#374151,stroke-dasharray:4 3 classDef planned fill:#FFFFFF,stroke:#9CA3AF,color:#6B7280,stroke-dasharray:6 4 classDef zoom stroke-width:3px class A,B,C,D,E,F,I,X basis class G,H store

    Onboarding goes through nine steps:

    1. Configure: the operator adds one file per source in sources/configured/. The file name is the stable source_id. The file names the transport, the location of the metadata, and the FSC Peer ID of the provider (source_configuration.go#L16-L28). It does not name the OIN or the organization name. These come from the certificate set.
    2. Discover the contracts: for the fsc transport, the reconciler looks in the existing FSC contracts. There it finds the metadata contract and the data contract of the configured peer. It does not discover sources: a contract without a source file activates nothing.
    3. Fetch or read: only the reconciler fetches source metadata. It uses ETag and If-None-Match. A 304 only extends freshness. The reconciler validates every 200 in full. The runtime never fetches metadata.
    4. Validate: the reconciler validates schema, origin, version, validity window, query, mapping, offers, claims, and the binding to the data contract. The source_oin in the document must equal the OIN in the certificate set (source-registry/onboarding/service.go#L403-L413).
    5. Candidate: a valid result becomes a complete candidate with state rollout_required. This candidate is not active. An invalid result does not replace the last complete candidate.
    6. Promote: an operator promotes a complete candidate set. In the demo, the reconciler can do this itself (--auto-promote). Promotion is a separate step (reconcile_command.go#L134-L151).
    7. Immutable release: promotion writes one release from the complete candidate set. The SHA-256 of the content identifies the release. A release never changes (postgresregistry/store.go#L300-L390).
    8. Active pointer: in the same database transaction, promotion sets the singleton active_release_id. If a promotion fails, the previous release stays active.
    9. Runtime reload: the readers poll the active pointer with a read-only role. They build the new release in memory and swap it atomically. The nl-wallet issuance server reads its configuration only at startup. So a new release needs a controlled restart of that server.

    Four readers use the active release:

    Reader What it derives Reload
    EUDI adapter source snapshot (source, query, mapping, FSC grant, validity window), Type Metadata, offer catalog /eudi-offers.json live, by polling
    Issuance init container issuance_server.toml: offers, disclosure, certificates, trust anchors at a restart of the issuance server
    ASIP per data service: query, attribute mapping, legal name of the authentic source, discovery records live, every 5 seconds (asi-provider/main.go#L101)
    Developer portal and landing page the offers that a citizen can start, from the adapter live

    The source registry is a shared module, services/source-registry (onboarding, postgresregistry, asisnapshot). The reconciler writes to it with the writer role. The adapter, the issuance init container, and the ASIP read it with the reader role. The reconciler has no Kubernetes API rights. It reads certificates and contracts and writes only to the registry.

    Transports¶

    A source has two legs: the metadata leg and the data leg. Each leg selects its own transport (service.go#L18-L28):

    Transport Metadata leg Data leg Authenticated
    fsc fixed path /.well-known/gbo through a separate FSC metadata service the data service named in the document, under its contract yes
    unsecured an absolute HTTP or HTTPS URL, with no FSC headers and no redirects an absolute URL no
    file a document in the metadata directory of the operator (--metadata-dir). The path cannot leave that directory not possible: a file cannot answer a query no

    Five rules apply when the two legs combine transports:

    • If no data_access block is present, the data leg uses the metadata transport.
    • fsc metadata with unsecured data is refused.
    • file metadata needs an explicit data_access.
    • If both legs use fsc, the two services must differ.
    • provider_peer_id is on the leg that speaks FSC, never on both.

    The registry reports both legs separately, as transport_authenticated and data_transport_authenticated (service.go#L56-L66). A single flag hides an FSC-authenticated data call whose description came over an unauthenticated channel. The party that controls the document decides the query, the mapping, and the wallet claims.

    The intended form is fsc on both legs. The other combinations are for an onboarding phase:

    • file is for a source that publishes no /.well-known/gbo. The operator then keeps the description of the product of another party. This is an exception under D-13. The transport flag makes the exception visible, and expires_at makes it temporary.

      The exception is admissible only with recorded agreement of the bronhouder (AV-08, F-71). The demo does not record this agreement. The need for agreement is only an instruction in source-metadata/README.md.

    • unsecured is for local demonstrations. Only the local compose file mounts that source (sources/local-demo/). Deployments use only sources/configured/.

    Four bounds stay in place with every transport:

    • The Peer ID comes from the GBO configuration.
    • The grant hash pins the contract.
    • The reconciler compares the OIN with the certificate.
    • Promotion is a separate step.

    The trust model for each transport is an open point in demo issue #221.

    Contract and activation¶

    A valid FSC contract does not take a source into use. It also does not put the offer of the source in the wallet (REQ-65, F-58). Transport and mandate are two decisions with two owners. If a contract alone activates a source, admission becomes automatic again through a back door (F-55). Each situation has a fixed result:

    Situation Result
    Valid metadata contract, no source file nothing happens
    Source file, no metadata contract source blocked: METADATA_CONTRACT_NOT_FOUND
    Source file, no contract for the data service source blocked: DATA_CONTRACT_NOT_FOUND
    FSC Manager unreachable source blocked: FSC_MANAGER_UNAVAILABLE
    Validated candidate without promotion not active

    The reason codes are in service.go#L141-L152. Automatic promotion is off by default (reconcile_command.go#L197). Compose and the Helm example turn it on for the demo. Then the source file is the management action. Demo v0.9.0 does not build two things: control over who can do that action, and a record of the admission decision (PSA B-09 in the decision register, REQ-123).

    Versions, freshness and isolation¶

    Source metadata fails closed for each source and ages within fixed bounds. An operator can roll it back (REQ-66). The mechanism has five parts:

    • Freshness: a successful check is fresh for at most 15 minutes. After that, it is stale for at most one hour. At acceptance, a document must be valid for at least one more hour (source_metadata_cache.go#L10-L14). The issuance route shows X-GBO-Metadata-Cache: fresh|stale.
    • States per source: each source has one of five application states. Kubernetes conditions are a separate thing.
      • pending: the check started.
      • rollout_required: a complete candidate waits.
      • active: the source is in use.
      • stale: the refresh fails, and the previous snapshot is within grace.
      • blocked: no usable snapshot exists, or the grace is over.
    • Per-source refusal: if a source is past its grace, only the requests for that source get HTTP 503.
    • Version rule: activation refuses a lower version than the last validated candidate. It also refuses the same version with other content (source_registry_backend.go#L163-L175). The rule has no test (#610).
    • Rollback: an operator activates a stored release with activate-source-release --release-id. The command refuses a release that the adapter cannot load. An auto-promoter respects the rollback until new candidate content arrives.

    Demo v0.9.0 has two deviations from the isolation rule (#606):

    • Promotion needs a valid version of every configured source (registry.go#L133-L158). The aim of this design is that no source leaves the wallet offer without notice. As a side effect, one broken source freezes new releases for all sources.
    • The offer list /eudi-offers.json takes the shortest grace of all sources (source_release_runtime.go#L95-L100). So the list fails for all sources at the same time.

    Source releases have the lifecycle that policy bundles lack: validation before activation, bounded staleness, atomic promotion, and rollback (F-59). For the policy side, see Policy lifecycle and ADR-0021.

    A certificate set per source¶

    Every source has its own certificate set for issuance: issuer, reader (access), and status-list certificates. GBO never shares a set between sources and never substitutes one (REQ-58). The issuer name and the purpose that the wallet shows are bound to the signing and reader certificates. A fallback to the set of another source made the wallet show the wrong issuer (F-50).

    If material is missing, onboarding fails hard for that source only:

    Situation Result
    No set for the source_id source blocked: CERTIFICATE_SET_NOT_FOUND
    Set without OIN or organization name source blocked: CERTIFICATE_SET_INVALID
    Mounted material differs from the active release GBO generates no issuance configuration (issuance_release.go#L113-L116)
    Two sources behind one FSC peer each source has its own set

    The reconciler gets only public leaf certificates and public CA certificates. Only the issuance init container gets the private keys of the leaf certificates. Provisioning is a separate privileged command. For where these certificates come from and how they map to EUDI trust roles, see Identity and trust.

    The source document¶

    The document is JSON, validated against gbo-source-metadata-v1.schema.json. The format is closed: validation refuses unknown fields. The envelope has these fields:

    Field Meaning
    schema_version 1.0 or 1.1. Version 1.1 adds the asi capability (#L17-L23)
    source_oin 20-digit OIN. It must equal the OIN in the certificate set
    version Numeric version. One version identifies one content
    issued_at, expires_at Validity window. At acceptance, at least one hour must remain
    capabilities.eudi attestations for EUDI issuance
    capabilities.asi attributes for verification through the ASIP (1.1 only)

    The eudi capability: claims once, Type Metadata generated¶

    Each attestation has type_id, type_version, offers, graphql, mapping_profile, display, and claims. Four of these fields hold structured content:

    • offers are the concrete wallet offers, each with fixed parameters (for example jaar: 2024). A request with parameters outside the published offers is refused with HTTP 400.
    • graphql holds service_reference, endpoint, one read operation in document, subject_variable, declared parameters, and result_pointer.
    • display is keyed by language. It holds a name, a description, a summary with {{claim}} placeholders, and rendering.
    • claims defines each claim once. A claim has one gbo-simple-v1 rule in source (pointer, datatype, optional optional), a label, an optional description, and sd (always by default, allowed, or never).

    Earlier versions had separate mapping, attribute_schema, and type_metadata blocks. The format removed them. GBO derives the mapping from claims. It generates the SD-JWT VC Type Metadata from display and claims (type_metadata.go#L64). Each Type Metadata field has a fixed origin in the document:

    Type Metadata Derived from
    name, description the first language in display
    display[] display, with lang from the key
    claims[].path, svg_id the claim name
    claims[].display[] label and description
    claims[].sd sd
    schema.properties source.datatype (date becomes a string with format: date)
    schema.required every claim without optional: true, plus vct and vct#integrity

    Because the schema comes from the same rules as the projection, a source cannot publish a schema that differs from what the mapping fills. Five validation rules apply to the claims (source_claims.go#L216-L242):

    • A summary placeholder must be a claim name.
    • Validation refuses reserved names (vct, vct#integrity, iss, status, cnf, iat, nbf, exp, sub, attestation_qualification).
    • The order of the claims is the order in which the wallet shows them.
    • Validation refuses the datatype number for EUDI, because nl-wallet v0.5 cannot show a non-integral value.
    • Only scalar datatypes pass. GBO does not support nested claims (REQ-78).

    The VCT of a type version is /types/{source-id}/{type-id}/v{type-version}. The value vct#integrity covers the exact bytes that GBO serves at that URL. A change to claims or display changes those bytes, so the change needs a new type_version. GBO never deletes published type versions automatically.

    For how an answer of the source becomes an attestation, and for the error codes if the answer does not fit, see ADR-0017 (REQ-116).

    The asi capability (schema 1.1)¶

    From schema 1.1 on, a source can also describe the attributes that it offers for verification through the ASIP (ADR-0039, Q-38). The asi capability has three parts:

    • authentic_source: the legal name and the country. The ASIP uses them in responses and discovery records (REQ-94).
    • graphql: one query that ends in only ...Selected, the subject variable, and the result pointer. For each request, the ASIP replaces ...Selected with the fields of the requested attributes (REQ-92).

    • attributes: for each attribute, an identifier, an optional type condition on, and fields. Each member of the value has exactly one operation:

      Operation Meaning
      pointer copy a field
      join with separator concatenate two or more fields, without empty parts
      const a fixed value of the member type
      each with pointer for each element of a list, the field at pointer

    The identifier must exist in the attribute catalog of GBO, schemas/asi-attributes.json. The catalog gives a value_schema for each identifier. The identifiers are placeholders until the EU catalog of attributes exists (Q-31).

    The profile gbo-simple-v1 applies only to the eudi capability. The asi capability composes values, because a source cannot always deliver a catalog value with a copy. For example, a house number is three BRP fields. The BRP document shows this composition (brp-graphql-server/config/gbo-source-metadata.json#L204).

    Onboarding applies six rules to asi (source_registration.go#L396-L406):

    • If asi has an error, onboarding refuses the whole source, also if eudi is valid. The active release stays.
    • The asi query uses the same data service as the attestations: one document, one data service.
    • Onboarding also refuses a document with only asi, because onboarding requires the issuance certificate sets.
    • If the reconciler cannot read the catalog, it refuses only the sources with asi.
    • A source with asi gets release snapshot version 4.0. A source without asi stays at 3.0.
    • Onboarding validates only the form. It does not validate the GraphQL schema of the source, or whether the policy of the source allows the selection. A difference becomes visible at the first request.

    If the description is absent, has no asi, or is stale, the ASIP answers 503 for verify, retrieve, and discovery (REQ-93). If no registry is available, the ASIP can read a release file (asi-provider write-release-file).

    Connection conditions for bronhouders¶

    GBO asks three things of a bronhouder, as candidate connection conditions:

    • The bronhouder publishes a machine-readable, versioned description for each data service at the fixed location. The description includes the read API of the logbook of the bronhouder (AV-07).
    • If the bronhouder has no endpoint of its own, it agrees provably with the description that the operator keeps (AV-08).
    • The bronhouder provides a certificate set that carries its OIN and organization name (REQ-67).

    Open points¶

    Seven points are open:

    • The document is not signed. The origin depends on the authenticated transport plus the OIN from the certificate set.
    • The description lacks three items: the read API of the logbook of the source, a reference to the DCAT-AP-NL description, and central findability (F-57, F-68, AV-07). Without the read API, a caller cannot fill dpl.read.nextLogbookId from the description.
    • DvTP does not use the description. The DvTP offer of a source is in the GBO rules. DvTP scope comes from the demand side. EUDI scope comes from the supply side (F-74).
    • Traceability of versions: no record shows which versions of the mapping, the source schema, and the attestation schema an attestation used (REQ-124).
    • Key custody: the central issuance server holds the private keys of the issuer and status-list certificates of every source (Q-17).
    • ASI resource list: in demo v0.9.0, the ASI authorization server takes its data services from configuration. It does not use the descriptions (#592).
    • Scale: how many sources the ASIP must connect, and how fast, is open (Q-38, sub-question 1).

    Traceability¶

    • Requirements: REQ-58, REQ-64, REQ-65, REQ-66, REQ-67, REQ-78, REQ-92, REQ-93, REQ-94, REQ-116, REQ-123, REQ-124, AV-07, AV-08
    • Findings: F-50 (closed), F-55 (closed), F-57 (open), F-58 (closed), F-59 (closed), F-68 (open), F-71 (open), F-74 (open)
    • Open questions: Q-17 (open), Q-19 (answered), Q-31 (open), Q-38 (partly answered)
    • Demo increments: SL-32 (done), SL-46 (done), SL-49 (done)
    • Decisions: ADR-0016, ADR-0017, ADR-0039

    Identity and trust¶

    GBO must know which organization it deals with, and which certificate the chain uses for which purpose. The design keeps two questions apart:

    • Who is this organization? This is the legal identity (OIN and name) and the technical identity on FSC.
    • Which certificates does EUDI need? These are the trust roles of attestation issuance and of the Authentic Source Interface.

    The capabilities are S04 and F1, under P-07 (trust through recognized admission and trust anchors). These decisions apply:

    • ADR-0003: FSC for all connectivity.
    • ADR-0023: part A, organization identity (accepted), and part B, EUDI certificate roles (proposed).
    • ADR-0028: PuB-EAA productization (proposed).

    For the requirements, see Identity, trust and transport.

    Authorization per request is a separate layer. FSC establishes the organization, but this tells nothing about what the organization can do in one request. For more information, see Authorization.

    Three identity carriers¶

    An organization in the chain has three identifiers (F-60):

    Carrier What it identifies Source
    FSC Peer ID the FSC peer: the system that sends or receives FSC traffic subject.serialNumber of the FSC certificate
    OIN the legal organization (bronhouder, consumer) serialNumber of the organization's certificate
    Organization name the legal name that a wallet or a record shows exactly one O attribute of the same certificate

    If the bronhouder runs its own peer, its Peer ID is its OIN. In other cases, the two values can differ. One peer can offer services of more than one bronhouder. Simulation Peer IDs are not OINs, for example 0000009950HYPBV00000. Until SL-49 (PR #242), the demo used one field for both values. In demo v0.9.0, the source configuration keeps provider_peer_id as a separate field (source_configuration.go#L35-L44).

    It is open whether policy can read the Peer ID of a consumer as its OIN. The alternative is that policy takes that link from the admission register (toelatingsregister) (Q-68).

    The legal identity comes from the certificate¶

    A GBO component can put the OIN or name of a bronhouder in an attestation or a decision record. The component takes that value from verified certificate material. A value that an operator can fill in freely is never the source (REQ-67, ADR-0023, part A).

    The certificate content decides the result:

    Certificate Result
    20-digit OIN in serialNumber, exactly one organization name The OIN and the name come from the certificate
    The configured OIN or name differs from the certificate Refused: the component does not load the set
    No 20-digit OIN, or not exactly one organization name Refused (CERTIFICATE_SET_INVALID)

    The rule is in development_ca_provider.go#L280-L288 and source-registry/onboarding/service.go#L293-L297. The source document also names its source_oin. This value must equal the OIN in the certificate set. If it differs, the onboarding refuses the document (Source onboarding). The issuer name, the description, and the logo that the wallet shows also come from the certificate (PR #321).

    This rule has these consequences:

    • The runtime gets leaf material and public CA certificates, but never CA private keys. Provisioning is a separate privileged command.
    • Consents are bound to the identity of the consumer. If that identity changes, the consents become unusable. The migration in PR #244 and PR #277 showed this.
    • In the default demo onboarding, the Belastingdienst peer publishes RvIG with the Belastingdienst OIN. This is a demo shortcut, and it does not show one OIN per bronhouder. The certificate sets still differ per source.

    Every channel goes through FSC¶

    Every channel that calls a source for an external party goes through FSC, with a valid certificate (REQ-46, ADR-0003). DvTP, EUDI issuance, and the ASIP each call through their own Outway. FSC traffic is mTLS between peers. The Manager of the provider issues the access token with the grant hash of the contract.

    FSC refuses a connection with an expired or revoked certificate. open-fsc checks revocation with a CRL cache. An operator can switch off this cache per Inway, Outway, and Manager. The requirement forbids this. The demo does not check this behavior. It is open within which time a revocation must take effect (Q-53).

    Private parties¶

    A private consumer authenticates in two ways, with separate roles (Q-06, answered):

    • People use eHerkenning at onboarding and for management (FR-03).
    • Systems use an organization certificate from a recognized issuer, linked to the OIN or the KvK number (FR-33, FR-34).

    The candidate connection condition has two parts (AV-04):

    • A private consumer runs its own FSC peer with a PKIoverheid certificate.
    • The private consumer uses the OIN as its legal identity.

    FR-33 allows an OIN or a KvK number. The link between OIN, KvK, and eIDAS identifiers is an open S04 decision. The trust framework for private parties as a whole is PSA decision B-09 in the decision register.

    An integrator connects under FSC delegation. The consent binds the party that the integrator represents (ADR-0034). The consent does not bind the integrator.

    The PKIoverheid question¶

    The first version of ADR-0023 aimed at one infrastructure, with PKIoverheid as the anchor for all certificates, including EUDI. GO and PSA no longer follow that ambition (Q-07, answered). The roles are separate:

    • PKIoverheid is the Dutch PKI for mTLS, FSC, and organization identity.
    • A PuB-EAA carries a qualified electronic seal, from a certificate that a QTSP issues. Neither PKIoverheid nor an access CA seals it (F-66).
    • An access CA issues access certificates only (ETSI TS 119 411-8). An access certificate authenticates an issuer or relying party to the wallet. It never signs attestations.

    Dutch EUDI governance decides which party operates the Dutch access CA. This is a dependency outside the decision scope of GBO.

    EUDI issuance: a certificate set per source¶

    The issuance facility keeps a certificate set per bronhouder. The set has issuer, reader (access), and status-list certificates. The facility never signs with the set of another bronhouder (REQ-58). The issuer name and the purpose that the wallet shows are bound to these certificates. A fallback to the set of another source made the wallet show the wrong issuer (F-50).

    A missing or incomplete set blocks only that source. For the failure cases, see Source onboarding.

    EUDI trust roles¶

    GBO issues attestations for bronhouders. Each of these bronhouders needs its own certificate per role, and one certificate never fills two roles (ADR-0023, part B, proposed, F-81). The roles are as follows:

    Role Purpose Issued by Trust anchor
    Organization or system certificate mTLS for FSC, and the OIN and name PKIoverheid PKIoverheid root
    Access certificate Authenticates the issuer to the wallet (OpenID4VCI) An access CA (ETSI TS 119 411-8) The access CA that the member state notifies
    Registration certificate Proves the registration, per registered service (since Implementing Regulation (EU) 2026/1730) A provider that the member state appoints Published by the member state
    Qualified certificate for electronic seal Seals the PuB-EAA. Profile ETSI TS 119 412-6 clause 8. Names the authentic source and the legal basis. Key in a QSCD A QTSP Open (Q-30)
    Status-list certificate Signs the status list for revocation Open (Q-17) Open

    ADR-0028 sets the roles and responsibilities around these certificates:

    • Each bronhouder is the PuB-EAA provider of its attestations. GBO operates the technical issuance facility. GBO is probably the EEAIssuer in the notification of each bronhouder. It is open who designates the Dutch PuB-EAA issuer, and who supervises (Q-28).
    • The issuer registers as relying party with the entitlement PUB_EAA_Provider.
    • It is open on which trust list PuB-EAA providers appear. The options are a List of Trusted Entities (ETSI TS 119 602) or the trusted lists (ETSI TS 119 612). The specifications contradict each other (Q-30). No decision exists for either list.
    • It is open who holds the seal and status-list keys. The options are the central facility, a remote signing service, or an HSM at the bronhouder (Q-17). In the demo, the central issuance server holds them.

    To verify the PID that the wallet discloses, the issuance server also trusts PID issuers. Its list of PID trust anchors holds these CAs (issuance_server.toml.example#L3-L9, issuance_release.go#L120-L121):

    • The BZK pre-production PID issuer CA.
    • The GBO development issuer CA.
    • The issuer CA of every source.

    That list is too broad. It must hold PID-provider anchors only. The callback from the issuance server to the adapter has no caller authentication (REQ-45, ADR-0018).

    ASI trust roles¶

    In the ASI route, the QTSP is not an FSC participant. The chain on FSC starts behind the ASIP (F-87). Two trust points apply:

    • Admission of a QTSP: only a QTSP with the QEAA_Provider right in the register becomes a client of the ASIP (REQ-88). That register and the certificate profile do not exist in demo v0.9.0 (F-85). It is open which identifier links the access certificate of a QTSP to its register entry (Q-35).
    • The seal on a result: the ASIP seals every verification result (REQ-83). The format is open (Q-32, ADR-0041). The demo seals with a development certificate. This certificate is not a qualified seal certificate.

    ADR-0037 describes the ASI front door.

    Demo PKI and production¶

    The demo generates its own trust anchors. Git ignores the private keys, and the demo generates them again for each checkout.

    The demo and production use different PKI parts:

    Area Demo Production
    FSC group root A self-hosted CA: cfssl with a root and intermediate CA (GBO-DEMO Root CA) (fsc-infra/pki/generate-root-ca.sh) PKIoverheid
    FSC certificate requests The FSC ca-certportal in front of cfssl (fsc-infra/docker-compose.yml#L60-L72) The PKIoverheid issuance process of each organization
    Organization certificates Per organization, a group certificate with serialNumber = OIN, and internal mTLS certificates (bootstrap-bd-mock.sh#L48) PKIoverheid certificates of each organization
    PDP AuthZEN endpoint A self-signed certificate that the Inways pin as CA (generate-pdp-cert.sh) An organization certificate
    EUDI issuer and reader CAs Two pre-provisioned development CAs. The demo never generates them, and onboarding stops without them (Makefile#L268-L272) A QTSP for the seal, an access CA, and a registration certificate provider
    Source leaf certificates The development CA provider mints source-bound issuer, reader, and status-list leafs, under a separate privileged command (Makefile#L326-L336) Issued per bronhouder, per role
    ASIP seal and QTSP client certificates From the same development CAs (Makefile#L276-L283, #L320-L324) A qualified seal certificate, and access certificates of admitted QTSPs
    PID trust anchor The BZK pre-production PID issuer CA The notified PID providers

    In the demo, the development CA fills all EUDI roles at the same time. Production separates the roles. The demo is not tested against these standards (F-81):

    • ETSI TS 119 471.
    • The certificate profile.
    • The checks of ETSI TS 119 472-3.

    Open points¶

    These points about identity and trust are open:

    • Can policy read the Peer ID of a consumer as its OIN (Q-68)?
    • The trust list for PuB-EAA providers (Q-30).
    • Custody of the seal and status-list keys (Q-17).
    • Designation of the Dutch PuB-EAA issuer, and supervision (Q-28).
    • The identifier between a QTSP access certificate and its register entry (Q-35).
    • The time limit for a revocation to take effect (Q-53).
    • The trust framework for private parties (PSA B-09).
    • Migration from the self-generated demo CAs.

    Traceability¶

    • Requirements: REQ-45, REQ-46, REQ-58, REQ-67, REQ-83, REQ-88, AV-04
    • Findings: F-50 (closed), F-60 (closed), F-66 (closed), F-81 (open), F-85 (open), F-87 (open)
    • Open questions: Q-06 (answered), Q-07 (answered), Q-17 (open), Q-28 (open), Q-30 (open), Q-32 (open), Q-35 (open), Q-53 (open), Q-68 (open)
    • Demo increments: SL-34a (done), SL-34c (done), SL-49 (done)
    • Decisions: ADR-0003, ADR-0023, ADR-0028 (proposed)

    Policy lifecycle¶

    Each bronhouder owns, writes, and publishes the policy that its own PDP evaluates. GBO supplies a reference policy set, an engine choice, and guidelines. GBO does not supply a central policy service. The following sections show how a policy travels from version control to a decision in demo v0.9.0, and which points are open.

    The policy lifecycle realizes capability S06. The decision is ADR-0021. For the management-plane scenario, see Policy distribution.

    Ownership per bronhouder¶

    The PAP and the PDP are at each bronhouder. The PDP is behind the FSC Inway of the bronhouder, and the management function serves only that PDP. The policy belongs to the source (P-10).

    The question of who can manage and publish the policy of a bronhouder has an answer: the bronhouder itself (Q-21, October 28, 2026). PSA S06 sets the norm for publication control. The norm asks for these items:

    • An owner.
    • An approver.
    • An effective date.
    • A change history.
    • Tests before publication.
    • An emergency and rollback procedure.

    Authority over policy is with competent public parties. As a result, GBO sets no requirements on the policy installation of another party. The management practices are guidelines (RL-01 to RL-05, in the guidelines table later on this page). A guideline becomes a requirement only if GBO delivers the management setup itself (Policy management guidelines).

    In the demo, all components run in one compose stack. This is a demo artifact and makes no statement about the architecture.

    Policy authoring¶

    All authorization policies are Rego in version control (policies/), with tests next to the rules. The set has four parts:

    Part Files Role
    Entrypoint authz.rego The package that OpenFTV evaluates. It maps the engine response to allow and reason
    Engine and readers gbo/engine.rego, gbo/lib.rego, gbo/consent.rego, gbo/graphql_schemas.rego Generic machinery: regime and service binding, the closed world, reason codes, the consent proof, schema pins
    Rules gbo/rules/dvtp/, gbo/rules/eudi/, gbo/rules/asi/ One package per access verdict: DVT0001, LVG0001, EUD0001, EUD0002, ASI0001
    Contract policy fsc/autosign.rego Contract acceptance for the provider's FSC Manager (ADR-0015)

    A new access verdict is a new rule file with tests. The engine does not change. For the rule model, see Authorization.

    Scripts generate two files, and CI checks them:

    • The schema pins (scripts/gen-graphql-pins.sh).
    • The rule list that the developer portal shows (scripts/gen-rules-json.sh). OpenFTV has no data API, so the portal reads a generated file.

    Validation before activation¶

    The PDP compiles the policy set as a whole. One bad module does not give a deny. Instead, it breaks every decision (F-52). The demo had this type of fault several times:

    • A stale policy declared the same package as an existing rule. Every request got HTTP 500.
    • A non-Rego file under policies/ silently removed every policy after it in walk order.
    • A second file with the same name replaced the first, because the PAP keys policies by file name.
    • The PAP reports a module that does not compile as loaded, while the old policy continues to decide (#151).

    The local safety net is make policy-check (Makefile#L92-L106). It refuses non-Rego files and duplicate file names under policies/. Then it runs opa check. Every make target that starts the PDP depends on it.

    make policy-test adds opa fmt --diff and opa test (Makefile#L115-L117). CI repeats these steps. CI also checks that the generated files are up to date (ci.yml#L135-L182).

    Validation and a visible fallback at activation are not built (RL-05). If a PDP gets a broken bundle, it does not keep the last valid set. It also does not report that a later version did not load. Source metadata has this lifecycle in demo v0.9.0: validation before activation, atomic promotion, and rollback (F-59, REQ-66). For policy, this lifecycle is a backlog item.

    The contract policy is in the same set. As a result, one broken module also stops the admission of new participants. The contract policy has a fixed package name (doelbinding.auto_sign_contract). If someone renames it, it resolves to nothing, and every contract stays pending.

    Distribution¶

    The demo distributes policy in two modes:

    Mode How When
    Mount (default) The PDP image carries the policies (Dockerfile#L62-L67). Compose mounts ./policies over them (docker-compose.yml#L157) Every make demo* target. Edit and save while you write Rego
    Bundle (opt-in) The OpenFTV Manager stores the policies in Postgres. Bundle gbo-pdp collects every policy with tag gbo-authz, with a version. If PDP_BUNDLE_MANAGER is set, the PDP pulls the bundle at start (docker-compose.yml#L145-L149) make demo-manager, make manager-seed
    sequenceDiagram autonumber box rgb(237,233,254) Version control participant GIT as Version control (policies/) end box rgb(241,239,232) Deployment participant SEED as seed-openftv-manager.py<br/>(deployment identity) participant IDP as Keycloak (realm gbo) end box rgb(220,252,231) GBO Basis participant MGR as OpenFTV Manager (PAP) participant PDP as OpenFTV PDP end box rgb(237,233,254) Records participant PG as postgres-ftv end SEED->>IDP: token request (deployment identity) IDP-->>SEED: short-lived access token SEED->>GIT: read policies/**/*.rego SEED->>MGR: POST/PUT /v1/policy/{id}, tag gbo-authz MGR->>PG: store policy and audit trail SEED->>MGR: GET /v1/policies: what left version control? SEED->>MGR: PUT /v1/policy/{id}, tag gbo-retired Note over SEED,PDP: make demo-manager restarts the PDP PDP->>MGR: GET /v1/bundle/gbo-pdp (internal port) MGR-->>PDP: bundle {version, policies} PDP->>PDP: compile and activate the whole set PDP->>PG: decision records to the ADL

    Version control is the source of the content. The Manager is the distribution mechanism. Policy enters the Manager only through its API. An administrator in the management interface uses the same path.

    The distribution has these properties:

    • The PDP pulls, and nothing pushes. The PDP authorizes its own management endpoints with the decision policy. That policy denies every request that is not a data request, so a push gets 403 (F-51, gbo-pdp.yaml#L18-L32). The bundle has no push targets. The PDP pulls at start, so a new seed needs a PDP restart.
    • The seed script retires policy and does not delete it. A delete fails upstream on a foreign key to the audit trail. The seed script removes the bundle tag from every policy that left version control (seed-openftv-manager.py#L116-L122). Without that reconciliation, a renamed rule stays in the bundle (RL-04).
    • Cedar policies authorize the management API. The Manager authorizes its own API with Cedar policies, separate from the Rego decision policy: admin.cedar, auditor.cedar, and pdp-bundle.cedar. Since OpenFTV v0.1.0, the bundle pull runs through the same authorizer. The PDP shows no identity, so pdp-bundle.cedar allows only GET on the one bundle path (RL-02).
    • The Cedar store seeds once. The Manager seeds its Cedar policies into Postgres only while the store is empty. After that, the Manager uses the store as the source of truth. An existing volume does not pick up a changed Cedar file (CHANGELOG). While its policy store is empty, the engine switches authorization off.
    • Writing and publishing are separate. The realm has the roles admin, author, and auditor. Publication uses a non-personal deployment identity with a short-lived token (RL-03).
    • The bundle has no signature. The bundle has an ID and a version. A bundle gets a signature only when it crosses an organization boundary. Inside one organization, signing is not planned (#426, closed as not planned). If a bronhouder lets another organization build or host its bundles, signing and verification become a requirement (F-09).

    Two components have the name Manager. The OpenFTV Manager manages policy. The FSC Manager manages contracts and issues access tokens. Always name which Manager you mean.

    The ADL database (postgres-ftv) runs in every profile, because the PDP does not start without it. Only the OpenFTV Manager, its management interface, and Keycloak are opt-in.

    Policy data¶

    Rules use data from four sources, each with its own lifecycle:

    Source Examples Lifecycle
    In the rule allowed_years of EUD0001, designated_issuers shared by the EUDI rules (eudi_helper.rego#L13-L20), the asip peer of ASI0001 Changes with the policy set
    In the bundle Schema digests per FSC service (graphql_schemas.rego) Generated from the bundled schemas. CI checks drift
    PIP pull Admission register: active, allowed_source_peer_ids, integrator mandates acts_for (dvtp-onboarding.yaml) Refreshed every 5 seconds
    Per request The consent proof and its status, resolved by the policy itself (consent.rego) Status live, keys cached 300 seconds (Consent)

    A place on a PID actor list (designated_issuers, asip) is an admission decision with authorization weight. In every environment, those lists must stay disjoint from the consent consumers (F-70, Authorization). In demo v0.9.0, the lists are policy data and not register data.

    Guidelines for bronhouders¶

    Each guideline has a demo status in demo v0.9.0:

    Guideline Demo status
    RL-01 Deliver policy as a versioned bundle. Do not bake it into the PDP Opt-in only (make demo-manager). The default mounts the policies. No signature
    RL-02 Authorize the management API with its own policy set. Deny on an empty store Built for the Manager (Cedar). The PDP itself does not obey it (F-51). The engine opens up on an empty store
    RL-03 Separate writing from publishing. Publish with a non-personal, short-lived identity Deployment identity built. The author role grants no action, so writing and publishing are not separate
    RL-04 Withdraw policy, and do not delete it. Reconcile with version control Built: retire_stale at every seed
    RL-05 Validate a bundle before activation. Fall back visibly to the last valid set Local check built (make policy-check). Visible fallback not built

    Each guideline is a SHOULD for the bronhouder. A promotion rule names when the guideline becomes a requirement.

    Policy version and the decision record¶

    The decision record must name the policy version that decided (REQ-59). This is not built. The ADL records show no policy version, also when the PDP runs on a versioned bundle. Without the version, nobody can trace a decision back to the rule text.

    Withdrawn policy stays in the Manager. This is a precondition for the trace (RL-04). For the ADL itself, see Logging.

    Divergence: Rego, not ODRL¶

    PSA S06 names ODRL as a policy language option. GBO uses Rego for every decision, and the OpenFTV Manager uses Cedar for its own API. GBO keeps this choice. Risks and technical debt records the deviation. Per D-13, the deviation must go to the standards bodies. It is open how the reference policy shows that it is not tied to one language or engine (Q-78).

    Traceability¶

    • Requirements: RL-01, RL-02, RL-03, RL-04, RL-05, REQ-59, REQ-66
    • Findings: F-09 (closed by ADR-0021), F-51 (open), F-52 (open), F-59 (closed), F-70 (open)
    • Open questions: Q-02 (answered), Q-21 (answered), Q-78 (open)
    • Demo increments: SL-13 (done), SL-44 (done)

    Logging, audit and traceability¶

    Every data exchange must be reconstructable afterwards: who asked for what, under which basis, with which decision, and which organization processed which personal data (P-12, capability S09). The record and correlation model on this page is the model that gbo-demo v0.9.0 implements. The decisions behind the model are ADR-0035 (correlation), ADR-0036 (decision records), and ADR-0026 (processing records).

    A controller (Verantwoordelijke) is the organization that is responsible for a processing under the GDPR. A data subject (Betrokkene) is the person whom a processing is about.

    Three records, one chain¶

    Logius maintains three related logging standards. Each standard records a different thing. GBO uses all three, together with traces and logs (F-63):

    Record Standard What it records Writer Store in the demo Role
    Decision Authorization Decision Log (ADL) each PDP evaluation the PDP (OpenFTV) Postgres database ftv_adl authoritative
    Processing Logboek Dataverwerkingen (LDV) 1.0.0 each processing of personal data each component, in the logbook of its controller one logbook per controller authoritative
    Transport FSC-Logging (draft) each FSC transaction FSC Inway and Outway transaction log per FSC peer authoritative
    Traces OpenTelemetry (OTLP) technical operations all services Jaeger, 7 days observability
    Logs none operational log lines, including the console decision log of the policy engine all services Loki, 7 days observability

    A PDP decision is not a processing, so it gets no LDV record. The LDV records are at three processings (F-64):

    • the consent status lookup at the register
    • the decryption at the source gateway
    • the query at the source

    Traces and logs are for debugging. They are sampled or best-effort, and nobody cites them as evidence. The audit records are in separate stores with their own guarantees (REQ-32, OBSERVABILITY.md). The components write their records to these stores:

    flowchart LR C[Consumer backend] -->|traceparent T<br/>Fsc-Transaction-Id X1| OW[Consumer Outway] OW --> IW[Source Inway] IW -->|AuthZEN| PDP PDP -->|status lookup<br/>T, X1| CR[Consent register] IW --> GW[Source gateway] --> SRC[Source GraphQL] C -.-> LA[(Consumer logbook<br/>LDV)] GW -.-> LS[(Source logbook<br/>LDV)] SRC -.-> LS CR -.-> LT[(Consent logbook<br/>LDV)] PDP -.-> ADL[(ADL<br/>decision)] OW -.-> TX[(FSC transaction logs)] IW -.-> TX %% GBO diagram palette: the same colors as the Globaal Ontwerp classDef basis fill:#DCFCE7,stroke:#16A34A,color:#0F172A classDef dvtp fill:#FEDCD8,stroke:#E28F80,color:#1E293B classDef eudi fill:#FFEDD5,stroke:#EA580C,color:#0F172A classDef source fill:#DDEBF7,stroke:#6F94B8,color:#1E293B classDef ext fill:#F1EFE8,stroke:#5F5E5A,color:#444441 classDef store fill:#EDE9FE,stroke:#7C3AED,color:#1E1B4B classDef mock fill:#F3F4F6,stroke:#9CA3AF,color:#374151,stroke-dasharray:4 3 classDef planned fill:#FFFFFF,stroke:#9CA3AF,color:#6B7280,stroke-dasharray:6 4 classDef zoom stroke-width:3px class C ext class OW,IW,PDP,GW basis class CR dvtp class SRC source class LA,LS,LT,ADL,TX store

    Correlation: trace ID and transaction ID¶

    Two identifiers link the records (REQ-55, ADR-0035):

    W3C trace ID Fsc-Transaction-Id
    Made by the application that starts the processing the FSC Outway (or the entry component)
    Count per processing one one per FSC transaction
    Recorded in LDV trace_id, ADL trace_id, spans, operational logs FSC transaction log, ADL adl.fsc.transaction_id, span attribute gbo.fsc.transaction_id

    Four rules apply to correlation:

    • Every component takes the trace ID unchanged from the incoming traceparent. The component sets the span of the caller as parent only for a caller in the same trace. It sends traceparent and tracestate on every outbound call.
    • The component looks for the trace ID in a fixed order: traceparent, then Fsc-Transaction-Id, then X-Request-Id, then the ambient span. If none of these is present, it starts a new trace (tracecontext.go#L78, #L181).
    • The transaction ID never replaces an incoming trace. A component that starts or receives an FSC transaction records the transaction ID next to the trace ID.
    • If an entry component receives no traceparent, it can tie its new trace to the UUIDv7 transaction ID that it mints (consumerhttp.go#L166-L182). If a request crosses FSC once, the trace ID and the transaction ID then have the same value. After a second FSC hop, they differ.

    The earlier rule "trace ID equals transaction ID" (ADR-0019) broke in three cases (F-67):

    • a caller that sends its own traceparent
    • one processing that calls several sources
    • every extra FSC hop

    FSC forwards traceparent on the data path. One hop breaks the context: the Inway calls the PDP over AuthZEN on a fresh context, with only X-Request-Id (F-39, F-41).

    The Inway copies the headers of the original request into the AuthZEN context. When the policy calls the consent register (toestemmingsregister) for a status, it reads the trace from this context. The status request carries the trace ID of the request with a new span. It also carries the transaction ID (consent.rego#L190-L245). As a result, the LDV record of the register lands in the trace of the request.

    The status lookup goes through the own Outway of the PDP. It is a second FSC transaction, but it sends the transaction ID of the consumer. FSC-Logging says that a transaction ID is unique per transaction. Nobody checked on a running stack whether the Outway accepts a duplicate ID from the client.

    Separate units of work keep separate traces. The consent_id joins consent issuance and the later query. The two do not share a trace (F-16).

    In most services, operational logs carry the trace ID through structured logging (graphql-server/slogctx.go#L15-L24). Logs and traces join on equal identifiers. Time stamps play no part in the join. In demo v0.9.0, the operational logs of bron-sidecar, eudi-adapter, and asi-provider carry no trace ID.

    Decision records (ADL)¶

    The PDP writes one ADL record for each evaluation, to the Postgres database ftv_adl (REQ-71, ADR-0036). The PDP does not start without this database, so the ADL runs in every deployment profile (docker-compose.yml#L117-L126). Contract-acceptance decisions are ADL records too. A reader gets a SELECT-only role, adl_reader (adl-reader.sql).

    The embedded OPA also writes a console decision log line for each evaluation. This line goes to Loki. It holds the full policy result: for each field, the rule that granted or denied it, and the step trace. The line is observability data. The developer portal shows it as detail next to the ADL record. The portal sets the color of the PDP from the ADL record alone (F-53).

    The ADL record holds the AuthZEN request and answer. OpenFTV takes only allow and reason from the policy. On a deny, reason becomes reason_user.en (authz.rego#L42-L51). Per-field detail cannot go in the answer, because the FSC Inway returns the reason to the consumer. So the record can hold only what the consumer can also see (F-72).

    The decision record has five known gaps:

    • No correlation behind the Inway: the Inway sends neither traceparent nor Fsc-Transaction-Id to the PDP. The record gets a random trace and no adl.fsc.transaction_id. A reader finds the record through the request headers stored in it (adl.go#L48-L66, #369). The fix is upstream in open-fsc.
    • No policy version: the records carry policies: 0 (REQ-59). A reader cannot see in the record which policy decided. For more information, see Policy lifecycle.
    • Only {allow, reason}: the record lacks the consent status answer (adl.core.information) and the configuration (F-72). Because the policy fetches the consent status during evaluation, nobody can replay a decision from the record.
    • No pointer to the consent logbook (Q-25). For more information, see Reading a chain.
    • A BSN in the EUDI and ASI routes. For more information, see Data handling.

    Processing records (LDV)¶

    Every GBO-delivered component that processes personal data writes one LDV record per processing and per data subject. It writes to the logbook of its own controller (REQ-72, ADR-0026). Only trace metadata crosses an organization boundary. A shared logbook breaks this rule, so the demo runs one ldv-logboek image as seven logbooks (docker-compose.yml#L410-L598):

    Logbook Controller Writers
    logboek-afnemer Hypotheek-BV (demo consumer) dienstverlener-backend, integrator-backend
    logboek-ir Installatie Register (demo consumer) ir-backend
    logboek-bd Belastingdienst bron-sidecar, graphql-server
    logboek-brp RvIG brp-sidecar, brp-graphql-server
    logboek-lvg LVG lvg-sidecar, lvg-graphql-server
    logboek-toestemming GBO consent-register, consent-portal-backend
    logboek-eudi-adapter GBO eudi-adapter

    In production, GBO does not build these logbooks. Each controller runs its own logbook, and GBO ships the client (services/ldv-client). The client holds the parts that are the same everywhere: configuration, the acknowledged write, trace and span IDs, and the attribute map. It also decodes FSC claims and derives the data subject.

    Each record carries five elements:

    • Trace context, as defined in ADR-0035.

    • The data subject, never a BSN: dpl.core.data_subject_id names the data subject in the own identifier space of the controller. The field data_subject_id_type makes the type explicit:

      Type Meaning Used by
      consent-id the consent that the consumer acted under consumer
      logboek-pseudoniem HMAC over the BSN with a key of this controller sources, EUDI adapter
      portal-subject the reference that the consent portal (toestemmingsportaal) derives consent register and portal
      brp-persoon-id the own record ID of RvIG, for a person named in a certificate about another person RvIG only

    • A processing activity: processing_activity_id refers to a versioned, resolvable activity, for example bd-ib-2025@v1. Each logbook serves a stand-in register of processing activities (GET /verwerkingsactiviteiten). The logbook validates writes against this register. The stand-in has no legal status (Q-08).

    • A pointer to the next logbook: if a component calls another party, it sets dpl.read.nextLogbookId to the read API of that party. The consumer does this for each source call. The EUDI adapter does it on the attestation record. The portal points to BSNk. That value is a demo placeholder, because the BSNk mock has no read API.
    • The calling party: on a lookup over FSC, dpl.core.foreign_operation.processor names the FSC peer of the caller. At the consent register, this is the peer verified from Fsc-Authorization (client.go#L441-L452, REQ-76).

    The LDV integration rests on six design choices:

    • One record per data subject: a further data subject of the same processing gets a child record under the first record. In the death-certificate flow, every further person that the certificate names gets a child record (ldv_query.go#L218-L285). A query over several tax years gives one record per activity.
    • Each logbook has its own pseudonym space: the pseudonym key is per controller. The same citizen is not recognizable across the logbooks of different controllers. A source logs under its own pseudonym, never under a value that the caller sends (F-69). Since SL-51, no pseudonym travels in the chain at all.
    • The logbook refuses a BSN: it scans every write for a nine-digit run that passes the BSN checksum (elfproef). The scan covers all values, the record name, and the resource. The logbook refuses a match. The check is word-bounded, so a 20-digit OIN passes (validate.go#L141-L157).

    • Durable first, delivered after: a component stores the record in a local outbox, with an fsync, before its response leaves. It delivers the record afterwards with retries (outbox.go#L17-L38). A logbook outage delays records. It does not fail requests and does not lose records.

      If a component cannot store the record locally, it refuses the processing. The reason is that a withheld response does not undo a processing that already happened. The primary key (trace_id, span_id) makes a replay idempotent.

      The consent register keeps its outbox as a table in the same database as the consents. So a consent and its record commit in one transaction.

    • Separate write and read tokens: a component that can write cannot read with that token.

    • A local extension: the consent register, the portal, and the EUDI adapter write dpl.gbo.* attributes. This extension has no approval from Logius. The honest claim is "LDV core with a local extension" (Q-72).

    In demo v0.9.0, the ASIP writes no LDV records, although it is a GBO-delivered component that processes personal data.

    How to read a chain¶

    The LDV read extension is POST /data-processing-operations. It selects records by traceId, processingActivityId, or dataSubjectId. A read starts at the application that started the processing. From there, a reader follows nextLogbookId (docs/ldv/README.md). For one DvTP query, a reader does these steps:

    1. Call the consumer logbook with trace ID T.
    2. Follow nextLogbookId in the consumer record to the read API of the source.
    3. Call the source logbook with T. It returns the records of the source gateway and of the source.
    4. Use the transaction ID for the FSC transaction logs. Find the ADL record through the transaction ID in the stored request headers (#369).
    5. Call the consent logbook with T. No record points there.
    sequenceDiagram box rgb(241,239,232) Reader participant R as Reader end box rgb(237,233,254) Records participant LA as Consumer logbook participant LS as Source logbook participant ADL as ADL participant LT as Consent logbook end R->>LA: read traceId T LA-->>R: record, nextLogbookId = source R->>LS: read traceId T LS-->>R: gateway and source records R->>ADL: SELECT on transaction ID (request headers) ADL-->>R: decision record Note over R,LT: no pointer leads here (Q-25) R->>LT: read traceId T LT-->>R: status lookup record

    Two gaps limit this route (F-68):

    • The start is at a party that LDV does not bind. In DvTP, a private consumer starts the processing. Without its records, nobody knows which sources one processing touched. A consumer that calls two sources writes two records under one trace ID. Each record has its own pointer and its own transaction ID.

      The minimum for a consumer is trace context and the transaction ID (AV-01). LDV for the consumer is a candidate condition (AV-02). The demo consumer logs under the consent ID, because it has no citizen identifier (Q-27).

      The register records form a second index over the whole chain. Every source call leads to a status lookup, and the register logs this lookup with trace and consent ID.

    • The step from the decision to the consent logbook. The PDP writes only an ADL record and no LDV record. The ADL has no field like nextLogbookId. The demo applies option 3 of Q-25: a reader calls the consent logbook by trace ID. The chain view in the developer portal shows that logbook as "reached without pointer" (dev-portal-backend/ldv.go).

    A caller can fill nextLogbookId only if the source publishes the read API of its logbook. In demo v0.9.0, the source metadata does not carry this API. The consumer and the EUDI adapter get it from configuration (REQ-64, Source onboarding).

    Citizen access works per controller, through the read extension of each logbook, by data subject. Each controller answers for its own processings (GDPR article 15) (F-65). Demo v0.9.0 does not build a view of the processings per consent.

    Data handling¶

    Logging holds no BSN that the processing does not need. Masking in the decision log is never the only safeguard (REQ-60). Each record type handles the BSN as follows, per route:

    Record Consent route (DvTP) EUDI and ASI routes
    LDV no BSN. The logbook refuses one no BSN. The logbook refuses one
    ADL and console decision log a placeholder, no identity (SL-51) the plain BSN, from the PID or the token
    Spans and operational logs no BSN no BSN

    In the consent route, the PDP input holds a placeholder for the subject. The source gateway replaces the placeholder after the allow (ADR-0033, Pseudonymization).

    In the EUDI and ASI routes, the query variables hold the plain BSN (eudi-adapter/source_metadata.go#L273, asi-provider/internal/graphqlsource/source.go#L94). Neither decision log masks anything. The ADL has no masking option, and the console log ignores the OPA mask policy (F-54).

    Earlier, the request mapper pseudonymized the BSN before evaluation. PR #370 removed this step when the mapper became a pure mapper. Until #368 decides, the demo accepts the BSN in both decision logs. The proposal is to keep identifiers out of the PDP input (ADR-0043).

    Protection and retention¶

    REQ-32 requires three things of audit records: protection against change and deletion, no sampling, and separation from operational logs. Demo v0.9.0 has this status for each property:

    Property ADL LDV logbooks FSC transaction logs
    Separate store yes yes, SQLite per logbook, synchronous = FULL yes, per peer
    Never sampled yes yes, acknowledged per record yes
    Read access SELECT-only role read token intra-organization API or the remote Manager (F-42)
    Tamper evidence (WORM, hash chain, notary) no no no
    Retention period not set not set not set

    Two points are open: who can read which records, and how long the records are kept (Q-08). The ADL source-reference model adds a constraint: a source that a record points to must stay available as long as the record exists.

    Architecture decisions

    Architecture decisions¶

    The decision log holds every architecture decision of GBO in MADR format. It contains the decisions of the archived reference architecture v0.6.2. It also contains the decisions that the GBO team made during the build of the demo.

    Each ADR names the PSA or GO constraint that it satisfies and the deliberation that produced it. Each ADR also links to its implementation in gbo-demo at release v0.9.0. A "Traceability" section at the end of each ADR lists the requirements, findings, open questions, and demo increments that the ADR depends on.

    If a later decision replaces an earlier one, both stay in the log. At the top of its body, the superseded ADR gives the reason. It keeps its text as history.

    The column "Serves" names the main requirements of each decision. The full list is in the ADR.

    Accepted

    ADR-0001: GraphQL as the source access interface¶

    • Status: accepted
    • Date: 2026-08-24 (ported from reference architecture v0.6.2)
    • Satisfies: P-02, D-09, GO: GraphQL as a selective query mechanism
    • Deliberation: Reference architecture v0.6.2, decision 1, and its GraphQL + PBAC proposal (archived and unpublished)
    • Implemented in: services/graphql-server, services/brp-graphql-server, services/lvg-graphql-server

    Context and problem statement¶

    Data minimization (dataminimalisatie) requires a different set of fields for each consent scope. With REST, each scope needs a separate endpoint or separate filter parameters. Policies must then also state who can use which filter. As a result, the API layer and the policy layer hold the same logic twice.

    Decision¶

    Bronhouders expose GraphQL endpoints. The selection set of the consumer is the data minimization: the query names exactly the fields that the consumer wants. The policy engine authorizes that query field by field.

    Selectors that matter for authorization, such as the belastingjaren year filter, must travel inside the query. Then the PDP can enforce them.

    Consequences¶

    • The query is the authorization object. For more information, see ADR-0009 and ADR-0013.
    • GraphQL runs over HTTP, so FSC proxies it unchanged (ADR-0003).
    • GraphQL is not a recognized type of FDS data service (datadienst). ADR-0025 proposes to standardize it. The iWlz/nID production precedent supports the pattern.

    Traceability¶

    • Requirements: REQ-08, REQ-11, REQ-17
    • Findings: none
    • Open questions: Q-11 (answered), Q-14 (open)
    • Demo increments: SL-03a (done), SL-03b (done)

    ADR-0002: OPA/Rego in OpenFTV, the FSC Inway as PEP, AuthZEN with the FTV GraphQL profile¶

    • Status: accepted
    • Date: 2026-08-24 (updated 2026-11-02: includes the decision "the FSC Inway is the PEP")
    • Satisfies: S05, P-09, GO: consent and legal basis as an enforceable authorization mechanism
    • Deliberation: Reference architecture v0.6.2, authorization models analysis (archived and unpublished), F-35, Q-16, demo PR #60, PR #482, PR #337
    • Implemented in: fsc-infra/docker-compose.yml (Inway AuthZEN plugin, with body), services/openftv-pdp/Dockerfile (OpenFTV v0.1.0), mapper/ftvgraphql.go, services/ftv-graphql-mapper, docs/ftv-graphql-profile.md, policies/

    Context and problem statement¶

    GBO needs one policy engine and one PEP-PDP protocol for all routes. Then the authorization logic is in policy and not in application code.

    Every source also needs an enforcement point in front of it. The interface of that point is the same at every source, so bronhouders must know it.

    Decision¶

    The PDP is OpenFTV (Federatieve Toegangsverlening) release v0.1.0 with embedded OPA/Rego. The same PDP does two jobs:

    • It evaluates data requests. FSC Inways call it for these.
    • It decides on contract acceptance. FSC Managers call it for these (ADR-0015).

    The FSC Inway of the source is the PEP. There is no separate PEP service. The AuthZEN plugin of the Inway sends every request to the PDP as an AuthZEN question, with the request body (AUTHZEN_WITH_BODY=true). Then the Inway enforces the answer.

    The PEP-PDP interface is OpenID AuthZEN 1.0 (POST /authzen/v1/evaluation). For GraphQL, the request follows the FTV GraphQL profile for AuthZEN (ftv-graphql/0.1). The PEP passes the raw body unchanged and never parses it (REQ-42). The PDP side builds the field list (ADR-0013).

    Considered options¶

    The GBO team compared three places for the PEP:

    1. FSC Inway as PEP (chosen). Every call to the source already goes through the Inway, and the Inway has an AuthZEN plugin (F-35).
    2. A separate PEP service between the Inway and the source (the earlier pep-service). It duplicates the PEP role. It also adds a hop. If that hop is in the wrong place, a request can go around it.
    3. A PEP at the source gateway. The gateway then makes the decision call and does the substitution. Enforcement and data transformation then mix in one component.

    Consequences¶

    • All authorization decisions come from Rego policies. The policies are versioned in Git and have tests.
    • If the source gateway is reachable outside the Inway, a request can skip the decision. So the gateway must be reachable only through the Inway (REQ-04, ADR-0033).
    • The demo patches the FTV GraphQL profile mapper into the OpenFTV v0.1.0 build. Each patch step checks that it changed something. When the upstream project includes the profile mapper, the demo removes the patch (#331). CI keeps the PDP ref and the Manager image tags on one release tag.
    • The PDP writes every decision to the ADL (ADR-0036).
    • The PSA mentions ODRL in S06. This design does not use ODRL. Risks and technical debt tracks the deviation.
    • GBO follows the FTV GraphQL profile and AuthZEN. This answers the question of which profile GBO follows (Q-16).

    Traceability¶

    • Requirements: REQ-04, REQ-42, REQ-44, REQ-17. This ADR replaces the removed REQ-52.
    • Findings: F-02 (closed), F-27 (closed), F-31 (closed), F-35 (resolved in demo)
    • Open questions: Q-16 (answered)
    • Demo increments: SL-17 (done), SL-18 (done), SL-31 (done), SL-40 (done)

    ADR-0003: FSC for all domestic connectivity¶

    • Status: accepted
    • Date: 2026-08-24 (ported from the reference architecture, updated 2026-11-02 for REQ-46 and the ASIP peer, gbo-demo v0.9.0)
    • Satisfies: D-03, S04, P-07 (trust through recognized admission and trust anchors)
