    • Deliberation: Reference architecture v0.6.2, decision 6 (archived and unpublished), REQ-46
    • Implemented in: fsc-infra/docker-compose.yml (OpenFSC v2.4.0 group: a directory peer and nine organization peers, among them the ASIP peer …1200 at #L1664-L1669). Each channel has its own Outway in dienstverlener-backend/main.go#L82, eudi-adapter/main.go#L115, and asi-provider/main.go#L83-L85.

    Context and problem statement¶

    Bronhouders must implement one connectivity stack for all routes, and not one stack for each route.

    Decision¶

    FSC (Federated Service Connectivity) carries all domestic traffic. FSC gives these functions:

    • mTLS with group certificates
    • contracts with grant hashes
    • access tokens from the Manager of the provider
    • transaction logs for each hop

    A channel that calls a source for an external party uses its own FSC Outway with a valid certificate (REQ-46). FSC establishes the identity of the calling organization. The authorization of each request stays a separate layer (ADR-0031).

    External protocols end at the edge of GBO:

    • A bridge at the edge translates cross-border OOTS traffic to FSC (ADR-0020).
    • Wallet protocols end at the EUDI chain (ADR-0018). The EUDI adapter is an FSC consumer.
    • QTSP protocols (ETSI TS 119 478 clause 6.1) end at the ASIP (ADR-0037). The QTSP is not an FSC participant. The ASIP is an FSC consumer with a peer of its own (…1200), so the source sees the ASIP as the actor.

    Consequences¶

    • A bronhouder connects once (Inway plus contracts) and serves every route.
    • The Inway is also the PEP (ADR-0004).
    • No channel goes directly into a source service or into its authorization.
    • FSC refuses a connection with an expired or revoked certificate. open-fsc checks revocation with a CRL cache. The Inway, the Outway, and the Manager each have a switch that turns this check off. That switch must stay on. The demo does not check the revocation behavior.
    • FSC does not propagate W3C trace context. The correlation model of ADR-0035 compensates for this.

    Open points¶

    There is no decision on the time within which a certificate revocation or a suspension takes effect (Q-53).

    Traceability¶

    • Requirements: REQ-46
    • Open questions: Q-53
    • Demo increments: SL-34, SL-39, SL-42

    ADR-0004: Five authorization concerns, federated evaluation, no central authorization server¶

    • Status: accepted
    • Date: 2026-08-24 (updated 2026-11-02)
    • Satisfies: D-01, S05, P-01
    • Deliberation: Reference architecture v0.6.2, decision 5 (archived and unpublished), Q-02, Q-10, F-02
    • Implemented in: fsc-infra/docker-compose.yml (concerns ① ②), services/openftv-pdp and policies/gbo (concerns ③ ④ ⑤)

    Context and problem statement¶

    The question "May this request proceed" splits into five questions. Each question changes at its own rate and has its own decision makers:

    • organization identity
    • organization permission
    • access basis
    • data scope
    • request validity

    A central authorization server couples all five questions and is a single choke point.

    Decision¶

    GBO evaluates each concern where it belongs, federated per organization:

    • mTLS and PKI answer identity at every connection.
    • The FSC Manager of the provider answers permission when it issues a token. Contract acceptance itself is a policy decision (ADR-0015).
    • The PDP at the Inway of the provider answers access basis, data scope, and request validity for each request.

    There is no central authorization server. An FSC access token never contains consent. Instead, the consumer presents a consent proof, and the PDP verifies it for each request (ADR-0032). The regime follows from the evidence that the request carries (ADR-0031).

    For legal-basis routes (Gov-to-Gov), the design evaluates the legal basis (grondslag) locally from policy data, without a PIP call. The demo does not implement this path. The path needs its own positive evidence, because a declared flow is not sufficient (ADR-0031). For more information, see Risks and technical debt.

    Consequences¶

    • A revocation takes effect on the next request. No token needs to be invalidated.
    • In the consent regime, each request depends on two network calls:
      • the consent status, asked over FSC and never cached
      • the JWKS of the register, cached for five minutes
    • Concern ② also has a part at request time for integrators. A delegated call needs a mandate in the admission register (ADR-0034).
    • For the mapping of the concerns to the components, see Authorization.
    • The demo does not implement rate limiting (part of concern ⑤). Risks and technical debt tracks this gap.

    Traceability¶

    • Requirements: REQ-04, REQ-18, REQ-46, REQ-48, REQ-74
    • Findings: F-02 (closed), F-08 (closed)
    • Open questions: Q-02 (answered), Q-09 (answered), Q-10 (answered)
    • Demo increments: none

    ADR-0005: BSNk PP polymorphic pseudonyms for private-sector access¶

    • Status: accepted
    • Date: 2026-08-24 (updated 2026-11-02: BSNk only at consent time)
    • Satisfies: P-04, S03, PSA open decisions: choice of BSNk PP
    • Deliberation: Reference architecture v0.6.2, decision 4 (archived and unpublished), BSNk preconditions, F-75, demo #364, PR #469, PR #477
    • Implemented in: consent-portal-backend/bsnk (activate, transform, BSN authorization list), consent/portal.go (values per party), services/bsnk-mock (mock of the BSNk interface, also the sources' decryption component)

    Context and problem statement¶

    Private parties are not allowed to process the BSN. But DvTP lets them request data from government sources about a specific citizen. Plain encryption of the BSN still gives them a universal correlation key.

    Decision¶

    GBO uses the BSNk PP polymorphic pseudonym infrastructure and calls it only at consent time. The decision has these parts:

    • The consent facility (toestemmingsvoorziening) activates the BSN of the citizen once, into a PI and a PP. These belong to the consent facility only (BSNK-03). ADR-0040 (proposed) describes how the consent facility recognizes the citizen later.
    • At each consent, while the citizen is logged in (BSNK-04), the consent facility asks BSNk to transform the PI and the PP. BSNk returns values for each recipient OIN:
      • an encrypted pseudonym (VP) for every source
      • an encrypted identity (VI) only for a source on the BSN authorization list (BSNK-06)
    • The consent facility splits the call into requests of four parties at most (BSNK-05).
    • The values travel in the consent proof (ADR-0032). After the allow, each recipient decrypts its own value locally, with its own keys (ADR-0033).
    • BSNk is not in the query path. The consumer gets no identifier.

    Consequences¶

    • The values of different parties cannot be linked. No party outside government can derive the BSN.
    • The consent facility must be a recognized BSNk participant (BSNK-01, F-75, Q-26).
    • At consent, the parties, the key versions, and the form of the proof become fixed for the whole validity period (F-78).
    • Every recipient needs its keys in advance, as a step of admission (BSNK-09, #467).
    • A pseudonym for the consumer itself is optional. The demo does not build it (#478, Q-01).
    • The demo mock follows the BSNk interface, but uses JSON instead of SOAP (BSNK-11). The mock enforces the requester-only PI, the BSN authorization list, and the four-party limit. The mock does not encrypt, so anyone can read the values. The three demo sources share one OIN and one decryption component.
    • For the identifier flow at each boundary, see Pseudonymization.

    Traceability¶

    • Requirements: REQ-20, REQ-21, REQ-80, REQ-82, BSNK-01, BSNK-03, BSNK-04, BSNK-05, BSNK-06, BSNK-09, BSNK-11
    • Findings: F-15 (closed), F-75 (open), F-78 (open)
    • Open questions: Q-01 (partly answered), Q-26 (open)
    • Demo increments: SL-02 (done), SL-51 (done)

    ADR-0009: Closed-world per-field rules: the rule is the catalog¶

    • Status: accepted
    • Date: 2026-08-24 (updated 2026-11-02: plain-Rego rules bound by regime and service)
    • Satisfies: P-02, D-11
    • Supersedes: ADR-0008
    • Deliberation: engine.rego (design notes in comments), REQ-48, REQ-97, F-90, demo commit 80af776 (rules as plain Rego), PR #527 (service binding)
    • Implemented in: policies/gbo: engine.rego (regime and service binding), lib.rego (reads the request only), rules/, engine_test.rego (every rule names its services)

    Context and problem statement¶

    For each requested field, the PDP must decide whether an authorization basis covers the field. The PDP must do this without a separate catalog, because a catalog can drift away from enforcement.

    A field key (ParentType.field) is unique only within one schema. Two services can share a key: Query.ingeschrevenPersoon is in both bri and brp (F-90).

    Decision¶

    Each rule is plain Rego. A rule declares these items:

    • rule_id, regime (consent or pid), and services (the FSC services that the rule applies to)
    • covers_fields and covers_types: the fields that the rule can grant
    • its reasons to refuse: deny for the whole request and deny_field[i] for one field

    If a rule gives no reason, it grants the field. Each rule checks the actor and the scope itself (REQ-48). lib.rego only reads the request. It holds no checks.

    The engine binds rules to fields in four steps:

    1. Only the rules of the active regime bind (ADR-0031).
    2. Only the rules that serve the FSC service of the request bind. The service is the service_name from the FSC access token. The Manager of the source signed this token (REQ-97).
    3. A field binds to the rules that name its key. An argument-free leaf outside the root types also binds to the rules that cover its parent type.
    4. For each field, the first bound rule without reasons grants the field.

    The rule set is a closed world:

    • If no rule covers a field, the PDP denies the field with NO_APPLICABLE_RULE.
    • If the PDP cannot make the decision for a field, it refuses the field as RULE_NOT_EVALUABLE. The request then fails as a configuration error.
    • If the field list of a request is uncertain, the PDP denies the whole request (REQ-17, ADR-0013).

    The demo has five rules, as the following table shows:

    Rule Regime Service Grants
    DVT0001 consent bri Income declaration fields under consent
    LVG0001 consent lvg Ownership check at the LVG, scope lvg:vbo:eigendom
    EUD0001 pid bri Income statement (inkomensverklaring) to the wallet, years 2024 and 2025
    EUD0002 pid brp Death certificate (akte van overlijden) to the wallet
    ASI0001 pid brp BRP fields for the ASIP

    Consequences¶

    • One artifact defines what is allowed and why. A new access decision needs a new rule file with tests.
    • A test requires every rule to name its services. A rule for one service cannot grant a field of another service with the same key.
    • Consent per year works because each scope covers one year (bd:ib:2025). Also, the year selector must travel inside the query. If the filter is missing, the request fails closed.

    • Reasons have two layers (REQ-06):

      • The consumer and the ADL get only a client code, such as FIELD_NOT_PERMITTED.
      • The rule codes for each field go only to the console decision log for the operator, in a fixed order.

      For more information, see Authorization.

    • The service catalog (dienstencatalogus) with a legal anchor from ADR-0008 stays an open governance question. Risks and technical debt tracks it.

    • gbo-demo v0.9.0 has no test that makes sure that every rule checks the actor itself (#604).

    Traceability¶

    • Requirements: REQ-48, REQ-97, REQ-17, REQ-06, REQ-74, REQ-08
    • Findings: F-21 (closed), F-23 (closed), F-90 (resolved in demo)
    • Open questions: Q-14 (open)
    • Demo increments: SL-03b (done), SL-13 (done), SL-33 (done)

    ADR-0013: GraphQL request mapping in the PDP ahead of policy evaluation¶

    • Status: accepted
    • Date: 2026-08-24 (updated 2026-11-02: the mapper only maps)
    • Satisfies: P-02, S05
    • Supersedes: ADR-0012
    • Deliberation: REQ-17, REQ-42, demo #364, #330, PR #370, PR #371, PR #482, FTV GraphQL profile
    • Implemented in: mapper/ftvgraphql.go (OpenFTV adapter), services/ftv-graphql-mapper (profile mapper), schemas/pdp-mirror (schema per FSC service), graphql_schemas.rego (schema pins), scripts/check-schema-drift.sh

    Context and problem statement¶

    Rules need clean, typed facts about the request instead of a raw query string. These facts are the fields, with their parent types and with their arguments as the source executes them.

    The PEP passes the raw body unchanged (ADR-0002). So a component on the PDP side must turn the body into a field list. That list must be complete. If it is not complete, the PDP denies the request (REQ-17).

    Decision¶

    A request mapper inside the OpenFTV PDP implements the mapping function of the FTV GraphQL profile (ftv-graphql/0.1) and nothing else. The mapper does these things:

    • It parses the GraphQL body and builds the field list. The parent type of each field comes from the bundled schema of the FSC service of the request. The arguments are as the source executes them.
    • It accepts only a query operation. A mutation or subscription gives OPERATION_NOT_SUPPORTED.
    • It enforces these limits:
      • body: 1 MiB
      • nesting depth: 64
      • fragment definitions: 100
      • selection depth: 64
      • field records: 1000
      • aliased selections: 100
      • validation time: 1 second
    • If a step fails, it marks the request COVERAGE_UNVERIFIABLE with a subcode (for example PARSE_ERROR, LIMIT_EXCEEDED). The engine denies the request.

    The mapper does not verify the consent proof. It does not call BSNk, does not pseudonymize, and reads no flow. The policy verifies the consent itself (ADR-0032). The regime follows from the evidence (ADR-0031).

    The profile mapper is a separate Go module. A thin adapter connects it to OpenFTV.

    Consequences¶

    • Rules stay declarative. Parsing happens once, in one place, in tested Go code. The conformance vectors of the profile run as tests.
    • The PDP loads one schema for each FSC service. The policy bundle pins the digest of each schema and denies a schema that is not pinned (CONFIG_ERROR SCHEMA_MISMATCH). A CI job checks for drift between the pinned schema and the schema that the source executes.
    • The source gateway accepts only the request shape that the PDP evaluated (ADR-0033).
    • The mapper is a patch on OpenFTV v0.1.0. The patch stays until the upstream project includes the profile mapper (#331). For more information, see Risks and technical debt.
    • The mapper does not pseudonymize any more. So the EUDI and ASI routes put the plain BSN into the PDP input (ADR-0043, proposed).

    Traceability¶

    • Requirements: REQ-17, REQ-42, REQ-18, REQ-60
    • Findings: F-25 (closed), F-54 (open)
    • Open questions: Q-14 (open)
    • Demo increments: SL-03a (done), SL-18 (done), SL-31 (done)

    ADR-0015: FSC contract acceptance by policy¶

    • Status: accepted
    • Date: 2026-08-24 (updated 2026-11-02: ordered refusal codes, delegated grants)
    • Satisfies: S04, P-07
    • Deliberation: autosign.rego (design notes in comments), REQ-61, F-55, F-56, demo #491, PR #464
    • Implemented in: policies/fsc/autosign.rego (ordered checks), services/dvtp-onboarding-register, pip-pull/dvtp-onboarding.yaml, fsc-infra/docker-compose.yml (Manager autosign call)

    Context and problem statement¶

    An FSC Manager can sign all incoming contracts automatically, or it can require a manual review. Neither option scales to an admission model. DvTP participation is a governed status, and a provider must accept contracts only from admitted parties. Admission comes from a register and not from decision policy (REQ-61).

    Decision¶

    The Manager of each provider sends every submitted contract through the PDP. The AuthZEN autosign call of the Manager evaluates a dedicated contract-acceptance policy (package doelbinding.auto_sign_contract).

    The policy reads the admission register (toelatingsregister). OpenFTV pulls this register every 5 seconds (attributes name, active, allowed_source_peer_ids, acts_for).

    The policy accepts grant type 2 (service connection) and grant type 3 (delegated service connection, ADR-0034). It runs eight checks in a fixed order, and the first check that fails names the refusal:

    # Code Refuses when
    1 NOT_AN_AUTOSIGN_REQUEST The input is not a well-formed autosign request
    2 GRANT_TYPE_NOT_ALLOWED The grants are not all type 2 or all type 3
    3 NO_COUNTERPARTY The contract has no party other than the provider itself
    4 ADMISSION_REGISTER_UNAVAILABLE The PIP pull supplied no register
    5 PARTY_NOT_IN_REGISTRY A party is not in the register
    6 PARTY_NOT_ACTIVE A party is suspended
    7 SOURCE_NOT_ALLOWED The party is not admitted for this source peer
    8 DELEGATION_NOT_REGISTERED A delegated grant has no registered integration

    A missing register (check 4) differs from an empty register (check 5). An empty register is available data that admits nobody.

    After a refusal, the contract stays proposed, so it can be submitted again (REQ-63). The contract does not become rejected.

    Consequences¶

    • Admission is data. If an operator activates or deactivates a participant in the register, the contract outcomes change without a policy edit. The register deactivates participants and does not delete them.
    • The contract question ("may these parties connect at all") stays separate from the request question ("may this field be read now") on purpose (REQ-62). The request policy reads the same register only for integrator mandates.
    • The autosign input of the Manager carries only peer IDs and grant types. So the policy decides about the parties and not about the services. Admission per service is a known limitation (F-56). Risks and technical debt tracks it.
    • The Manager fixes the package name. If someone renames the package, the policy resolves to nothing and every contract stays pending.
    • A suspended consumer keeps its existing contract and can still send queries (REQ-110, Q-53). Changes to admissions are not logged (REQ-123).

    Traceability¶

    • Requirements: REQ-61, REQ-62, REQ-63, REQ-110, REQ-123, AV-06
    • Findings: F-55 (closed), F-56 (closed), F-52 (open)
    • Open questions: Q-22 (answered), Q-53 (open), Q-74 (open)
    • Demo increments: SL-09 (mostly covered), SL-45 (done)

    ADR-0016: Source-owned metadata and reconciliation-based onboarding¶

    • Status: accepted (mechanism). The document format is a proposal for PSA S10.
    • Date: 2026-08-24 (updated 2026-09-07 for the source registry and split transports in gbo-demo v0.6.11, and updated 2026-11-02 for the claims model, schema 1.1 with asi, the shared registry, activation, and certificate sets in gbo-demo v0.9.0)
    • Satisfies: P-10, D-04, S10, S07, S04
    • Deliberation: F-57, F-58, SL-46, docs/source-onboarding.md, docs/source-metadata-cache.md
    • Implemented in: eudi-adapter reconcile command, source registry backend, shared registry module services/source-registry (onboarding, postgresregistry, asisnapshot), gbo-source-metadata-v1 schema, certificate set per source in issuance_config.go#L159-L180, ASIP reader in asi-provider/main.go#L101

    Context and problem statement¶

    To connect a source, GBO must not need code on the GBO side or a central catalog of source capabilities. The source owns its schema, its queries, and its attestation definitions (REQ-64). Also, a valid transport contract alone must not be enough to take a source into use (F-58).

    PSA S10 leaves the content and the interface of the source-specific GBO configuration open. The following mechanism (publish, validate, activate, roll back) is a GBO design decision. The document format gbo-source-metadata-v1 is the proposal of the demo for that open S10 decision. It is not a final interface agreement.

    Decision¶

    Publication¶

    Each source publishes its own machine-readable metadata at /.well-known/gbo. The metadata is versioned, expires, and is validated against a schema. The GBO configuration names only where to fetch it. Identity comes from certificates. Access comes from FSC contracts.

    The document holds capabilities for each channel:

    • eudi (schema 1.0 and 1.1): for each attestation, type_id, type_version, offers, graphql, mapping_profile, display (per language), and claims. Each claim has one gbo-simple-v1 rule in source, a label, an optional description, and sd. GBO generates the SD-JWT VC Type Metadata from display and claims (ADR-0017). The document has no separate mapping, attribute_schema, and type_metadata blocks any more.
    • asi (schema 1.1 only): the attributes that a source offers to the ASIP (ADR-0039).

    For more information about the structure, see Source onboarding.

    Validation into a registry¶

    A reconciler validates the fetched metadata into candidate records in a PostgreSQL source registry. It validates the schema, the origin, the version, the validity window, and the binding to the data contract. The source_oin must equal the OIN in the certificate set. If it does not, the result is METADATA_INVALID.

    The registry is a shared module (services/source-registry). The EUDI adapter writes it. The adapter, the issuance configuration step, and the ASIP read it.

    Activation as a separate management action¶

    Activation is a separate management action (REQ-65). A valid FSC contract activates nothing. A source becomes active only through an explicit source configuration file, a validated candidate, and a promotion.

    If a configured source has no contracts, it is blocked with METADATA_CONTRACT_NOT_FOUND or DATA_CONTRACT_NOT_FOUND. If the FSC Manager is unreachable, the result is FSC_MANAGER_UNAVAILABLE. Automatic promotion is off by default. Compose and the Helm example turn it on for the demo.

    Releases¶

    Promotion creates one immutable release from the complete candidate set. It activates the release in the same transaction. The SHA-256 of the content document identifies the release.

    These products derive from the active release:

    • the adapter activation snapshot
    • immutable type metadata
    • the issuance-server configuration (an init step writes it)
    • the offer catalog
    • the description of each data service for the ASIP

    The runtime path never fetches metadata. The adapter and the ASIP poll the active release through a read-only database role.

    Lifecycle per source¶

    The lifecycle rules are in REQ-66. Metadata is fresh for 15 minutes at most and has one hour of stale grace. It must be valid for at least one hour.

    The source states are pending, active, stale, blocked, and rollout_required. If a source is past its grace, it gets HTTP 503. This applies to that source only. A lower version is not activated. The same version with other content is not activated either.

    Certificate set per source (fail-hard)¶

    Issuance keeps one certificate set for each bronhouder (REQ-58). The set holds the issuer, reader (access), and status-list certificates. Issuance never shares or substitutes a set.

    The checks fail hard:

    • If a set is missing, the source is blocked with CERTIFICATE_SET_NOT_FOUND.
    • If a set has no OIN or organization name, the result is CERTIFICATE_SET_INVALID.
    • If the mounted material differs from the active release, the configuration generation is blocked.

    If two sources are behind one FSC peer, each source gets its own set. The certificate binds the issuer identity and the purpose. So a shared set shows the wrong issuer (F-50).

    Transports¶

    The two legs of a source choose their transport independently:

    • The metadata leg (metadata_endpoint) is fsc, unsecured, or file. The file transport reads a document that an operator manages from a confined directory. It is for sources that publish no endpoint.
    • The data leg (data_access) is fsc or unsecured. If data_access is omitted, the data leg inherits the metadata transport.

    FSC metadata with unsecured data is refused. With file metadata, an explicit data_access is required. Both legs report their authentication status separately (transport_authenticated, data_transport_authenticated).

    Consequences¶

    • To onboard a source, an operator needs only configuration and contracts. There is no GBO catalog of sources, years, or schemas to maintain.
    • Version rollbacks, byte drift, and expired metadata are refused. If metadata is unavailable, issuance fails closed (HTTP 503).
    • Published versions of type metadata are immutable (vct#integrity covers the exact bytes). They are never deleted automatically. A change to claims or display needs a new type_version.
    • An operator can roll back with activate-source-release --release-id. An auto-promoter that watches the registry keeps that choice while the candidate set stays the same.
    • Two deviations from REQ-66 remain (ICTU/GBO-demo#606):
      • Promotion needs a valid version of every configured source. So one broken source stops new releases for all sources.
      • The offer list /eudi-offers.json takes the shortest grace of all sources and fails for all sources at once.
    • The version rule has no test (ICTU/GBO-demo#610).
    • The origin depends on the authenticated transport and the OIN from the certificate set. The document itself is not signed.
    • With the file transport, the operator maintains the description instead of the source. This is a D-13 exception. data_transport_authenticated makes the exception visible, and expires_at makes it temporary. The exception needs recorded consent of the bronhouder (AV-08, F-71). The demo does not record that consent.
    • If the GraphQL service of a source is already on FSC, the source can be onboarded before it publishes /.well-known/gbo. The data call stays bound to the contract.
    • The central issuance server holds the private keys of the issuer and status-list certificates of every source. There is no decision on whether that is allowed (Q-17).
    • The issuance server reads its configuration only at startup. A new release needs a controlled restart (state rollout_required).

    Open points¶

    The following points are open:

    • The description does not contain the read API of the logbook of the source, a reference to the DCAT-AP-NL description, or central findability (F-57, F-68, AV-07).
    • In demo v0.9.0, DvTP does not use the description. The DvTP offer of a source is in the GBO rules. The DvTP scope comes from the demand side (F-74).
    • Who can do the activation action, and how the admission decision is recorded (PSA B-09 in the decision register).
    • The final form of the source configuration. This is the open PSA S10 decision.

    Traceability¶

    • Requirements: REQ-64, REQ-65, REQ-66, REQ-58, REQ-67, AV-07, AV-08
    • Findings: F-50 (closed), F-57 (open), F-58 (closed), F-59 (closed), F-68 (open), F-71 (open), F-74 (open)
    • Open questions: Q-17, Q-19, Q-38
    • Demo increments: SL-46

    ADR-0017: Gbo-simple-v1 as the attestation mapping profile¶

    • Status: accepted
    • Date: 2026-08-24 (updated 2026-11-02: scope eudi only, claims model, error contract, gbo-demo v0.9.0)
    • Satisfies: S10, S11
    • Deliberation: docs/gbo-simple-v1.md, REQ-116
    • Implemented in: internal/gbosimplev1/profile.go, gbo-simple-v1 schema, claims validation in source_claims.go#L216-L242, generated Type Metadata in type_metadata.go#L64, error codes in profile.go#L33-L37, runtime in main.go#L302-L316

    Context and problem statement¶

    Source data must become attestation claims through a mapping. The source must be able to declare this mapping in its metadata. GBO must be able to execute the mapping without trusting logic from the source.

    The bronhouder stays responsible for the attestation content. So GBO must not add to the content or convert it (REQ-116).

    Decision¶

    GBO defines gbo-simple-v1 under a fixed URN. It is a mapping profile that is minimal on purpose and fails closed. The profile has these properties:

    • It projects one source object to flat claims through RFC 6901 pointers.
    • It has six data types and hard limits.
    • It has no conversions, filters, joins, defaults, expressions, or I/O.
    • Zero source rows give a no_data outcome (no credential). More than one row is an error.
    • Unknown mapping properties are refused.

    The profile applies only to the eudi capability of the source metadata. The asi capability has its own operations (pointer, join, const, each) against a value schema that GBO keeps (ADR-0039).

    Claims model¶

    A source defines each claim once, in claims. Each claim carries these items:

    • its gbo-simple-v1 rule as source (pointer, datatype, optional optional)
    • a label for each language
    • an optional description
    • sd (always by default, allowed, or never)

    GBO derives the mapping from the claims. GBO also generates the SD-JWT VC Type Metadata from display and claims. In this metadata, schema.required is exactly the non-optional claims, and every claim gets svg_id. The claim order is the display order in the wallet. Reserved claim names (vct, iss, status, cnf, and others) are refused.

    No partial attestation¶

    If the answer of the source does not fit the mapping, the adapter issues nothing. This includes the claims that do fit. The adapter gives these outcomes:

    Case Outcome
    A mandatory claim is missing HTTP 502, GBO_SIMPLE_PATH_MISSING
    A mandatory claim is null or has another type HTTP 502, GBO_SIMPLE_TYPE_MISMATCH
    The result is not a list HTTP 502, GBO_SIMPLE_RESULT_TYPE
    There is more than one result HTTP 502, GBO_SIMPLE_RESULT_AMBIGUOUS
    There is no result HTTP 404 (no_data), and the adapter still logs it
    An optional claim is missing or null The claim is left out, and the rest is issued

    The consumer sees only the HTTP status. The code is in the adapter log.

    Consequences¶

    • Mappings are data. They can be validated against a JSON Schema. They have an independent set of conformance fixtures (testdata/cases.json).
    • More expressive needs (derivations, unit conversions) require a later version of the profile and not ad-hoc extensions. A source that needs another form delivers that form itself.
    • A change to claims or display changes the integrity value of the Type Metadata. Therefore the change needs a new type_version.
    • The profile supports number, but EUDI onboarding refuses it. The reason is that nl-wallet v0.5 cannot show an amount that is not an integer. Risks and technical debt tracks this.

    Open points¶

    • The profile does not support nested claims (objects and lists) with selective disclosure for each element. Only scalar data types pass validation (REQ-78).
    • In demo v0.9.0, nobody can trace which versions of the mapping, the source schema, and the attestation schema an attestation used (REQ-124).

    Traceability¶

    • Requirements: REQ-64, REQ-78, REQ-116, REQ-124
    • Open questions: Q-20, Q-38
    • Demo increments: SL-46

    ADR-0018: EUDI issuance through disclosure-based OpenID4VCI on the nl-wallet stack¶

    • Status: accepted
    • Date: 2026-08-24 (updated 2026-11-02: no flow or subject identifier type, PID verification and the callback gap, gbo-demo v0.9.0)
    • Satisfies: P-06, S11, GO: PuB-EAA issuance
    • Deliberation: Reference architecture v0.6.2, PuB-EAA Provider (archived and unpublished), REQ-45, SL-25, demo constraints in AGENTS.md
    • Implemented in: services/eudi-adapter, services/eudi-issuance-server (nl-wallet v0.5.0), PID trust anchors in issuance_server.toml.example#L3-L9, adapter route in source_release_runtime.go#L69

    Context and problem statement¶

    Citizens must receive attestations from government sources into their EUDI wallet. The reference architecture called this function the shared PuB-EAA provider (PubEAA-voorziening). The protocol stack and the identification mechanism were open.

    PSA v1 treats the wallet as a hook (P-06). The demo proves the route, but the route is outside the v1 scope of the PSA.

    Decision¶

    GBO realizes the issuance function on the open-source nl-wallet issuance server (pinned version), with disclosure-based issuance. The issuance has five steps:

    1. The wallet discloses its PID over OpenID4VP. The issuance server verifies the disclosure against its PID trust anchors.
    2. The issuance server calls the GBO EUDI adapter (POST /attestations/{sourceID}/{typeID}). The adapter reads the BSN from the disclosed PID.
    3. The adapter gets the source data over FSC through the standard PEP-PDP chain. It uses the query from the source metadata (ADR-0016). The adapter is a channel adapter, and the PDP of the source decides (REQ-44).
    4. The request carries no consent proof. So the PDP evaluates it under the PID regime (ADR-0031). Grants carry no flow or subject_id_type property.
    5. The adapter projects the answer with gbo-simple-v1 (ADR-0017). The server issues the credential as dc+sd-jwt with immutable type metadata. It uses the certificate set of the bronhouder (ADR-0016).

    Consequences¶

    • Issuance is a full GBO route. It uses the same source API and the same authorization chain as DvTP. The source carries no logic that is specific to the wallet.

    • The issuance policy enforces three things:

      • the presence of a PID
      • an actor allowlist (designated_issuers)
      • limits for each type (EUD0001, EUD0002)

      These checks replace the abstract subject.bsn == resource.bsn rule of the reference architecture.

    • The issuance server verifies the PID. The demo removed a separate check in the adapter (SL-25). The demo does not test this verification independently.

    • The main gap is the callback from the issuance server to the adapter. The adapter route has no caller authentication. Any caller that reaches the adapter can post any BSN. The adapter then calls the source as the designated issuer peer, and the PDP allows the request. Nothing binds the BSN in the query to a verified disclosure (REQ-45, ICTU/GBO-demo#133). Risks and technical debt tracks this gap.
    • In addition to the PID providers, the PID trust list holds the GBO development CA and the issuer CA of every source.
    • The BSN from the PID stays in the PDP input and is in both decision logs (REQ-60, ADR-0043).
    • The validity is 365 days for every type. Each type has one status list. For the productization, see ADR-0028.

    Open points¶

    The following points are open:

    • Trust in the callback and positive PID evidence (Q-18, REQ-45). Two solutions meet REQ-45:

      • The adapter verifies the SD-JWT itself.
      • The issuance server authenticates the callback and delivers signed evidence.

      Both solutions also need the binding of the disclosure to the request. The PID trust list must hold only PID-provider anchors. A revocation check of the PID is a recommendation (SHOULD). The legal status of a BSN from a PID is part of Q-18.

    • Attestations about a related person. They follow a relation that the source declares, starting from the verified requester (REQ-57, F-47, Q-14). The demo uses a source view. The alternative is filter arguments that the policy requires with fixed values (ICTU/GBO-demo#425).

    • Validity and revocation for each type. The bronhouder sets them. If an attestation is valid for more than 24 hours and the source data changes, the attestation must be revoked. GBO has no change feed (REQ-77, F-82).

    Traceability¶

    • Requirements: REQ-44, REQ-45, REQ-57, REQ-58, REQ-60, REQ-74, REQ-77
    • Findings: F-47 (open), F-70 (open), F-82 (open), F-83 (open)
    • Open questions: Q-14, Q-18
    • Demo increments: SL-19, SL-25, SL-26, SL-29, SL-43

    ADR-0020: AS4 bridge for SDG-OOTS¶

    • Status: accepted (not implemented in gbo-demo v0.9.0)
    • Date: 2026-08-24 (ported from the reference architecture)
    • Satisfies: S08, GO pattern B, SDG regulation (EU 2018/1724)
    • Deliberation: Reference architecture v0.6.2, decision 7 and OOTS bridge (archived and unpublished)
    • Implemented in: not implemented. gbo-demo v0.9.0 has no implementation.

    Context and problem statement¶

    The Single Digital Gateway Regulation requires cross-border evidence exchange through the Once-Only Technical System (OOTS). OOTS uses eDelivery AS4 transport, OOTS-EDM payloads, and SMP discovery. This is an EU obligation, so GBO has no architectural choice here.

    Decision¶

    GBO builds an OOTS adapter at its edge. The adapter has three parts:

    • A Domibus access point receives AS4 messages.
    • An OOTS-EDM adapter maps evidence requests.
    • An FSC translator forwards the requests to bronhouders over the standard FSC and PEP-PDP chain.

    The bronhouder sees a normal FSC request. AS4 exists only at the edge, in line with the national Basisinrichting OOTS.

    Consequences¶

    • Bronhouders serve cross-border requests without work that is specific to OOTS.
    • The mapping of evidence types depends on canonical semantic models (ADR-0024).
    • The route needs a legal-basis policy path in the Gov-to-Gov style. This path is not implemented either. Risks and technical debt tracks both gaps.

    Traceability¶

    • Open questions: Q-79

    ADR-0021: Policy management and distribution per bronhouder¶

    • Status: accepted
    • Date: 2026-08-24 (proposed as "Policy distribution through a central PAP with signed bundles", rewritten and accepted 2026-11-02)
    • Satisfies: S06, D-01, P-10
    • Deliberation: Reference architecture v0.6.2, gap 1 "authorization policy lifecycle" (archived and unpublished), Q-21 (answered October 28, 2026), F-09, F-51, F-52, demo #426 (bundle signing, closed as not planned), PR #337
    • Implemented in: opt-in Manager profile: bundles/gbo-pdp.yaml, authz/pdp-bundle.cedar, scripts/seed-openftv-manager.py (retire, never delete), and validation in Makefile (policy-check, policy-test)

    Context and problem statement¶

    Each bronhouder runs its own PDP (ADR-0004). Someone must write the policy for that PDP, publish it, and deliver it to the PDP with integrity. The earlier proposal put a central PAP at GBO: a central registry, signed bundles, and governance in the GBO standards bodies.

    Q-21 asked who can manage and publish the policy of a bronhouder. The answer is that policy management stays with each bronhouder. The policy belongs to the source (P-10). Bundle signing inside one organization is not planned (#426).

    Decision¶

    • The PAP and the PDP are at each bronhouder. The bronhouder writes, approves, and publishes its own policy. GBO has no central PAP.
    • GBO supplies guidance and no service. The guidance is a reference policy set, the engine choice (ADR-0002), and the guidelines RL-01 to RL-05:
      • Deliver policy as a versioned bundle, and do not bake it into the PDP (RL-01).
      • Authorize the management API with its own policy set, and deny on an empty store (RL-02).
      • Separate writing from publishing. Publish with a non-personal, short-lived identity (RL-03).
      • Withdraw policy instead of deleting it. Reconcile the deployed set with version control (RL-04).
      • Validate a bundle before activation, and fall back visibly to the last valid set (RL-05).
    • A bundle is signed only when it crosses an organization boundary. Inside one organization, signing is not planned. If a bronhouder lets another organization build or host its bundles, signing and verification become a requirement.

    Considered options¶

    This decision compared three options:

    1. Policy management per bronhouder (chosen). This option fits P-10 and the federated PDP. Each bronhouder carries the governance cost.
    2. A central PAP with signed bundles (the earlier proposal). This option gives one place to author and approve policy. But it puts the policy of the bronhouder under another organization, and it needs signing across that boundary.
    3. Policy baked into the PDP image. This option has no lifecycle: no version, no withdrawal, and no validation before activation (F-09).

    Consequences¶

    • This decision closes the design gap of F-09: signing is required only across an organization boundary. The guidelines and their adoption remain.
    • The demo shows the guidelines with the OpenFTV Manager (opt-in, make demo-manager):
      • The bundle gbo-pdp is tagged and has a version. The PDP pulls it at start.
      • Seeding withdraws stale policies and never deletes them.
      • A Cedar policy limits the pull of the PDP to one bundle and to GET.
      • By default, the PDP loads ./policies from a mount.
    • Push distribution does not work. The PDP authorizes its own management endpoints with the decision policy. That policy denies everything that is not a data request (F-51). So the PDP pulls instead.
    • The policy store is cumulative and cannot delete. One duplicate or broken module stops every decision (F-52). Before every PDP start, make policy-check refuses non-Rego files and duplicate file names, and compiles the set. A visible fallback to the last valid set is not built (RL-05).
    • The ADL does not record the policy version that made the decision (REQ-59).
    • The PSA mentions ODRL. This mention stays a deviation (Risks and technical debt).

    Traceability¶

    • Requirements: RL-01, RL-02, RL-03, RL-04, RL-05, REQ-59
    • Findings: F-09 (closed by this ADR), F-51 (open), F-52 (open), F-59 (closed)
    • Open questions: Q-21 (answered)
    • Demo increments: SL-44 (done)

    ADR-0023: Organization identity from the certificate, and separate EUDI certificate roles¶

    • Status: accepted (part A, organization identity), proposed (part B, EUDI certificate roles)
    • Date: 2026-08-24, rewritten on 2026-11-02 for gbo-demo v0.9.0. The rewrite split the ADR into organization identity and EUDI certificate roles, and moved the BSNk production part out.
    • Satisfies: P-07 (trust through recognized admission and trust anchors), S04, S11, F1
    • Deliberation: reference architecture v0.6.2, gap 2 and trust model comparison (archived and unpublished), F-60, F-66, F-81, SL-49, and demo PR #242, PR #247, PR #321
    • Implemented in:
      • Part A: the OIN and the name come from the certificate in development_ca_provider.go#L280-L288. The refusal of a set without OIN or name is in source-registry/onboarding/service.go#L293-L297. The Peer ID is separate from the OIN in source_configuration.go#L35-L44.
      • Part B: not implemented. One development CA stands in for every role (issuance_config.go#L159-L180).

    Context and problem statement¶

    The first version of this ADR had one goal: a single "converged" trust and identity story. That story had three parts:

    • PKIoverheid as the basis for all certificates.
    • One common anchor for all organization identifiers.
    • The production BSNk PP.

    GO and PSA dropped that goal. P-07 does not name PKI any more (Q-07). Two separate questions remain.

    Question A is: who is this organization? The demo had three identity carriers side by side: the FSC Peer ID, a configured OIN, and the certificate. One field mixed two identities, and the runtime held CA private keys (F-60). Simulation Peer IDs are not OINs (0000009950HYPBV00000).

    Question B is: which certificates does EUDI issuance need? The analysis first confused the PuB-EAA seal and the access CA with PKIoverheid (F-66). Since August 2026, PuB-EAA issuance falls under ETSI TS 119 471. That standard has its own registration and certificate profile (F-81).

    The BSNk production part of the first version is not in this ADR. ADR-0005 covers pseudonymization. ADR-0040 covers citizen recognition and the BSNk participant.

    Decision¶

    Part A: organization identity (accepted)¶

    The decision for organization identity has five parts:

    1. The legal identity of a bronhouder (OIN and organization name) comes from its verified certificate material. It does not come from configuration (REQ-67). The OIN is the 20-digit serialNumber. The name is exactly one O attribute.
    2. GBO refuses a configured OIN or name that differs from the certificate. GBO also refuses a certificate without a 20-digit OIN, or without exactly one organization name.
    3. The configuration holds the FSC Peer ID separately from the OIN (provider_peer_id). One peer can offer services of more than one bronhouder.
    4. The runtime gets leaf material and public CA certificates, never CA private keys. A separate privileged command does the provisioning.
    5. FSC participants use PKIoverheid certificates (ADR-0003).

    Part B: EUDI certificate roles (proposed)¶

    GBO issues attestations for a bronhouder. Each such bronhouder needs its own certificates, one per role. One certificate never fills two roles. The roles are as follows:

    Role Purpose Issued by Trust anchor
    Organization or system certificate mTLS for FSC, and organization identity (OIN, name) PKIoverheid PKIoverheid root
    Access certificate Authenticates the issuer to the wallet (OpenID4VCI) An access CA (ETSI TS 119 411-8) The access CA that the member state notified
    Registration certificate Proves the registration of the service, one per registered service (since Implementing Regulation (EU) 2026/1730) A provider of registration certificates that the member state appoints Published by the member state
    Qualified certificate for electronic seal Seals the PuB-EAA. The profile is ETSI TS 119 412-6 clause 8. It names the authentic source and the legal basis (eIDAS art. 45f(1)(b)). The key is in a QSCD A QTSP Open: Q-30
    Status-list certificate Signs the status list for revocation Open: Q-17 Open

    PKIoverheid is not an EUDI access CA. It is also not the seal infrastructure for PuB-EAAs. An access CA issues access certificates only, and it never signs attestations. REQ-58 makes the certificate set per source fail-hard (ADR-0016).

    Consequences¶

    • An attestation and a decision record name the bronhouder with an identity that an operator cannot fill in freely.
    • Consents are bound to the identity of the consumer. If that identity changes, the consents become unusable. The migration in PR #244 and PR #277 showed that the binding is real.
    • In the default demo onboarding, the demo publishes RvIG through the Belastingdienst peer with the Belastingdienst OIN. That is a demo shortcut, so it does not show one OIN per bronhouder. The certificate sets still differ per source.
    • The demo development CA stands in for all EUDI roles at once. Production separates the roles.
    • The choice of the party that operates the Dutch access CA depends on Dutch EUDI governance. That choice is outside the decision scope of GBO.

    Open points¶

    These points are open:

    • Can policy read the FSC Peer ID of a consumer as its OIN, or must policy take that link from the register (Q-68)?
    • On which trust list do PuB-EAA providers appear: a List of Trusted Entities (ETSI TS 119 602) or the trusted lists (ETSI TS 119 612)? The specifications contradict each other (Q-30).
    • Who holds the keys of the seal and status-list certificates: the bronhouder, or the central issuance facility (Q-17)?
    • How does the migration from the self-generated CAs of the demo work?

    Traceability¶

    • Requirements: REQ-46, REQ-58, REQ-67
    • Findings: F-60 (closed), F-66 (closed), F-81 (open)
    • Open questions: Q-06, Q-07, Q-17, Q-30, Q-68
    • Demo increments: SL-34a, SL-49

    ADR-0026: Each controller logs its own processing in an LDV logbook¶

    • Status: accepted
    • Date: 2026-08-24, proposed as "Logboek Dataverwerkingen integration". Rewritten and accepted on 2026-11-02.
    • Satisfies: P-12, P-13, P-10, S09
    • Deliberation: reference architecture v0.6.2, gap 5 "traceability correlation" (archived and unpublished), REQ-72, F-64, F-65, F-68, F-69, and demo PR #303 (#302), PR #366, docs/ldv/README.md
    • Implemented in:
      • services/ldv-logboek: the logbook stand-in, one instance per controller.
      • services/ldv-client: the shared client (outbox.go).
      • validate.go: the BSN refusal.
      • docker-compose.yml: the seven logbooks.

    Context and problem statement¶

    A citizen and an auditor must be able to see which organization processed which personal data, and why. The decision log records decisions. It does not record processings, because a PDP decision is not a processing (F-63). The gap is at the processing itself (F-64):

    • The consent status lookup at the register.
    • The decryption at the source gateway.
    • The query at the source.

    The Logius standard Logboek Dataverwerkingen (LDV, v1.0.0) records each processing in the logbook of its controller (verantwoordelijke). Only trace metadata crosses an organization boundary.

    Decision¶

    The decision has four parts:

    • Every component that GBO delivers and that processes personal data writes one LDV record per processing and per data subject. The record goes to the logbook of the controller of that component (REQ-72).
    • The record carries these values:
      • The trace context, as ADR-0035 decides.
      • The data subject in the pseudonym space of that controller, with an explicit data_subject_id_type. The data subject is never a BSN.
      • A versioned, resolvable processing_activity_id.
      • dpl.read.nextLogbookId, if the processing calls another party.
      • The FSC peer that the Inway verified, if the component is a processor on a lookup over FSC (REQ-76).
    • GBO ships the client. Each controller owns its logbook (P-10).
    • A component stores the record durably in a local outbox before the processing delivers. If the logbook is down, the record arrives later. The outage never loses the record, and it does not fail the request.

    Considered options¶

    1. A logbook per controller, written by a shared client (chosen).
    2. One central GBO logbook. Not chosen: LDV keeps records at each controller, and only trace metadata crosses a boundary.
    3. OpenTelemetry spans, relabeled as LDV records. Not chosen: spans are sampled, and their delivery is not acknowledged (REQ-32).
    4. A failed request when the logbook is down (the first demo version). The outbox replaced this option, because a withheld response does not undo a processing that already happened.

    Consequences¶

    • The demo runs one ldv-logboek image as seven logbooks: Belastingdienst, BRP, consent (register and portal), EUDI adapter, consumer (Hypotheek-BV and the integrator), LVG, and Installatie Register. Twelve components write to them.
    • The decryption at the source gateway is a processing at the source. Each logbook uses its own pseudonym space. As a result, a pseudonym does not travel between the logbooks of different controllers (F-69).
    • LDV records never hold a BSN. The logbook refuses any record with a run of nine digits that passes the BSN check digit test (elfproef).
    • A reader follows a chain forward from the start logbooks through nextLogbookId. In DvTP the chain starts at the consumer, and LDV does not bind the consumer (F-68, AV-02).
    • The consumer has no citizen identifier, so it logs under the consent ID (Q-27).
    • Citizen access works per controller, through the read extension of each logbook (F-65). A view of the processings per consent is not built in demo v0.9.0.

    These points are open:

    • The register of processing activities is a stand-in without legal status. Retention and read access are open (Q-08).
    • Components write a local dpl.gbo.* extension that nobody ratified (Q-72).
    • No pointer leads from the decision at the source to the logbook of the consent register (toestemmingsregister) (Q-25).
    • In demo v0.9.0, the ASIP writes no LDV records.
    • Production needs WORM storage, hash chaining, or a notary for the logbooks (REQ-32).

    Traceability¶

    • Requirements: REQ-72, REQ-32, REQ-55, REQ-60, REQ-76, AV-02
    • Findings: F-07 (closed), F-63 (closed), F-64 (resolved in demo), F-65 (closed), F-68 (open), F-69 (resolved in demo)
    • Open questions: Q-08 (open), Q-24 (closed), Q-25 (open), Q-27 (open), Q-72 (open)
    • Demo increments: SL-50 (exploration done, build delivered)

    ADR-0031: The authorization regime follows from the evidence a request carries¶

    • Status: accepted
    • Date: 2026-11-02
    • Satisfies: S05, P-01, D-11
    • Supersedes: ADR-0030
    • Deliberation: REQ-74, F-70, Q-15, and demo #334, PR #363, CHANGELOG
    • Implemented in:
      • engine.rego (regime selection) and consent.rego (token read).
      • The rule regimes in dvt0001.rego, eud0001.rego, and asi0001.rego.
      • The tests in engine_test.rego.

    Context and problem statement¶

    The PDP judges a request under one of two regimes:

    • In the consent regime (DvTP), the consent of a citizen is the access basis.
    • In the PID regime (EUDI issuance, ASI), a verified PID disclosure of the citizen is the basis.

    Each regime has its own rules and its own reasons to deny.

    A component must select the regime. If the consumer selects it, the consumer chooses the basis for its own judgment. Earlier designs put the selection in three places:

    • A header.
    • A signed claim of the provider (ADR-0014).
    • An FSC grant property (ADR-0030).

    All three are a declaration about the request. None of them is evidence in the request.

    Decision¶

    The regime follows from the evidence that the request carries:

    • If a consent token is present (X-GBO-Consent-Token, verified or not), the request is in the consent regime. Only the rules with regime := "consent" bind: DVT0001 and LVG0001.
    • If no consent token is present, the request is in the PID regime. Only the rules with regime := "pid" bind: EUD0001, EUD0002, and ASI0001.
    • If two consent proofs are present, the policy denies with CONSENT_CONTEXT_INVALID. The policy does not pick one of them.

    Every rule declares its regime. Only the rules of the active regime bind, so the deny reason also comes from that regime. FSC grants carry no properties. No component reads a flow.

    Considered options¶

    1. Evidence in the request (chosen). The request carries no declaration that a party can forge or must maintain. Each rule still checks its own basis, so a wrong regime cannot give access.
    2. flow as an FSC grant property (ADR-0030). Both peers sign it, but it is a declaration per contract. Each consumer needs one contract per regime, and a change needs a new contract.
    3. Dispatch from component metadata or from the certificate (SL-24, dropped). This option binds the regime to the caller, and not to the request. A party that acts in both regimes does not fit.
    4. A request header or a default regime (SL-48). With this option, the consumer chooses the regime. Not chosen.

    Consequences¶

    • The rules already did the security work. DVT0001 and LVG0001 deny without a verified consent. The PID rules deny without a PID subject. The regime decides which reasons the PDP reports. The regime does not decide access. Engine tests pin the reason in both directions.
    • Only consent is positive evidence. A request enters the PID regime because it has no consent proof (F-70). For this reason, the PID regime needs its own positive evidence: a verified PID disclosure (REQ-45). In demo v0.9.0, the adapter callback that carries this evidence is not authenticated (#133).
    • The actor lists of the PID rules (designated_issuers, asip) must stay disjoint from the consent consumers in every environment. A test pins this for the seeded peers only (engine_test.rego).
    • A Gov-to-Gov regime on a legal basis needs its own positive evidence. It cannot be a third regime that rests on an absence.
    • The source gateway uses the same evidence. If a consent token is present, the source gateway takes the subject from it. If not, the source gateway passes the request through (ADR-0033).

    Traceability¶

    • Requirements: REQ-74, REQ-48, REQ-45, REQ-18
    • Findings: F-70 (open), F-32 (resolved in demo), F-43 (superseded), F-49 (premise lapsed), F-62 (resolved in demo)
    • Open questions: Q-15 (answered)
    • Demo increments: SL-24 (dropped), SL-48 (done)

    ADR-0032: The consent proof: signed, a value per source, a placeholder in the query, status online over FSC, verified in policy¶

    • Status: accepted
    • Date: 2026-11-02
    • Satisfies: S01, S03, S05, P-01, P-04
    • Supersedes: ADR-0007
    • Deliberation: REQ-68, REQ-79, REQ-80, F-44, F-61, and demo PR #238, PR #371 (#330), PR #390, PR #469, #383, #473
    • Implemented in:
      • consent_token.go: the proof.
      • consent.rego: the verification and the status check in policy.
      • status.go: the status listener behind the register Inway.
      • lib.rego: the placeholders.
      • docker-compose.yml: the status call over the PDP Outway.

    Context and problem statement¶

    In DvTP, the consent of the citizen is the access basis. The PDP at the source must establish three facts itself (REQ-68):

    • The consent comes from the consent register (toestemmingsregister) and is unchanged.
    • The consent is bound to this consumer, this data set, and this citizen.
    • The consent is valid at the time of the request, also after a revocation one second before.

    The consumer must not hold a citizen identifier (REQ-20). The consumer also must not choose the subject of its question (REQ-79). BSNk transforms values only while the citizen is logged in (BSNK-04). For this reason, the register must make every value that a source needs at consent time. These values travel with the proof.

    Decision¶

    The proof¶

    When the citizen gives consent, the consent register signs a JWT with these properties:

    • The algorithm is ES256. The header has typ=gbo-consent+jwt and kid. The public keys are in the JWKS of the register.
    • The claims are consent_id, scopes, scope_entries (per source), dienstverlener_oin, valid_until, iss, aud (default gbo:dvtp:pdp), iat, nbf, exp (equal to valid_until), and jti. The dienstverlener_oin is the represented party (ADR-0034).
    • The encrypted_subject claim holds a pseudonym (VP) per source OIN. If the source is on the BSN authorization list, it also holds an identity (VI) for that source. Each value carries its key_set_version. Only that source can read the value (REQ-80).

    The proof holds no PI and no BSN. If a proof has no pseudonym for every party, the register refuses it.

    The consumer¶

    The consumer sends the proof unchanged in X-GBO-Consent-Token (AV-05). In its query, the consumer names the citizen only with a placeholder:

    • consent:identity for a BSN API.
    • consent:pseudonym for a source-pseudonym API.

    Each rule lists the placeholders that it accepts. If the query has a literal value, or a placeholder without a verified proof, the PDP denies (CONSTRAINT_MISMATCH).

    The PDP policy verifies the proof itself¶

    The request mapper only maps (ADR-0013). consent.rego does these steps per evaluation:

    1. It verifies the ES256 signature against the JWKS of the register. The policy caches the JWKS for 300 seconds. On an unknown kid, the policy fetches the JWKS again.
    2. It verifies the claims in Rego, with 30 seconds of clock skew.
    3. Only after that, it asks the status of this consent_id. This call uses no cache and a 2-second timeout. It goes over FSC, through the Outway of the PDP, to the Inway of the register (FSC service consent-status).

    Keys can be five minutes old. The status cannot be old. Every failure maps to its own reason code:

    • CONSENT_SIGNATURE_INVALID
    • CONSENT_TOKEN_EXPIRED
    • CONSENT_KEYS_UNAVAILABLE
    • CONSENT_CONTEXT_INVALID
    • CONSENT_NOT_FOUND
    • CONSENT_STATUS_UNAVAILABLE
    • CONSENT_WITHDRAWN

    The policy ignores a pip.consent in the input.

    After an allow¶

    After an allow, the source gateway takes its own value from the proof. The gateway decrypts the value with its own keys and replaces the placeholder (ADR-0033).

    Considered options¶

    1. A signed proof, with the status online (chosen).
    2. Only a consent ID, and the PDP looks up the content at the register (ADR-0006). The register becomes the only source of the evidence. The consumer presents nothing that the PDP can verify.
    3. A status list that the PDP fetches periodically. A revocation takes effect only after the next fetch. REQ-14 needs a deny on the next request.
    4. A verifiable credential or presentation. This is a wallet format for a server-to-server proof. It adds a holder role that the consumer does not have.
    5. A PI in the query, and a BSNk call at the PEP or the source (ADR-0010, ADR-0007). The PI belongs to the requester only (BSNK-03). BSNk transforms only while the citizen is logged in (BSNK-04).
    6. Consent verification in the Go request mapper (the earlier demo). FTV puts attribute retrieval inside the PDP. With verification in the mapper, the decision rests on facts that the policy did not establish (REQ-18).

    Consequences¶

    • Freshness is asymmetric on purpose (F-61). The basis travels as a proof. The status stays online, so the register is a dependency on every request (REQ-75). The values for latency and availability are open (Q-47).
    • The status check is a processing at the register. The register answers only an FSC peer that its Inway authenticated. The register logs that peer as the processor (REQ-76). Any connected peer can still ask the status of any consent whose ID it holds. A restriction to the own PDP of the source is not built in demo v0.9.0.
    • A replay from (input, policy, data) is not possible. The policy fetches the status during the evaluation. The engine copies the resolved consent into its response for the console log. The ADL carries only {allow, reason} (F-72, ADR-0036).
    • The PDP verifies that the subject comes from the proof. The PDP does not verify who the subject is (F-77). One request names one subject. No policy can depend on the identity of the subject.
    • The proof freezes at consent (F-78). The parties, key versions, BSN authorization, and proof form stay fixed for its validity period. The proof has no version. If a source is added or gets new keys later, it needs a new consent, or it keeps its old keys (AV-09).
    • The proof is a bearer token. The actor binding stops use by another consumer, but it does not stop replay by the same consumer. Production needs a shorter validity and a proof-of-possession binding to the FSC identity (Risks and technical debt).
    • The consumer holds no citizen identifier (F-76). What the consumer records about "this person" hangs on the consent ID. A pseudonym for the consumer itself is not built (#478).

    These points are open:

    • Where does the signing key live, and how does it rotate (Q-55)?
    • Does the proof bind the purpose (Q-69)?
    • Is the integrator in the proof (Q-46)?
    • Who sets the validity period (Q-13)?

    The design came in three steps:

    1. A consent PIP through a PEP pre-fetch (SL-08).
    2. A signed, actor-bound proof (SL-47).
    3. An encrypted value per source and a placeholder (SL-51).

    Traceability¶

    • Requirements: REQ-68, REQ-75, REQ-76, REQ-14, REQ-18, REQ-19, REQ-20, REQ-21, REQ-79, REQ-80, REQ-82, AV-05, BSNK-03, BSNK-04
    • Findings: F-44 (resolved in demo), F-61 (closed), F-72 (open), F-76 (open), F-77 (open), F-78 (open)
    • Open questions: Q-05 (answered), Q-13 (open), Q-46 (open), Q-47 (open), Q-55 (open), Q-69 (open)
    • Demo increments: SL-08 (done), SL-23 (done), SL-47 (done), SL-51 (done)

    ADR-0033: The source gateway decrypts its own value after the allow, and only the Inway reaches it¶

    • Status: accepted
    • Date: 2026-11-02
    • Satisfies: P-04, P-10, S03, S07
    • Supersedes: ADR-0011
    • Deliberation: REQ-21, REQ-81, F-30, F-37, F-79, and demo #364, PR #469, PR #476, PR #477, #473
    • Implemented in:
      • bron-sidecar/main.go: the gateway acts on the consent proof.
      • substitution.go: the own value and the recipient check.
      • decryption.go: the source keys, with older versions kept.
      • transport.go: only the request shape that the PDP judged.
      • docker-compose.yml: the network isolation.

    Context and problem statement¶

    Under a consent, the query of the consumer names the citizen with a placeholder (ADR-0032). The source API needs a BSN, or the own pseudonym of the source for the citizen. A component must replace the placeholder, under three conditions:

    • Only after the PDP allowed the request (REQ-04).
    • Inside the boundary of the source, with the keys of the source, and without a central party in the query path (REQ-21).
    • Without a BSNk call, because BSNk transforms only while the citizen is logged in (BSNK-04).

    A transformation after the decision is a gateway task. It is not a policy task (F-37).

    Decision¶

    A gateway that the source owns (bron-sidecar) sits between the source Inway and the source API. The gateway works as follows:

    • The evidence decides. If a consent token is present, the subject comes from the token. Without a token, the request passes through unchanged (PID regime, ADR-0031). Grant properties play no part.
    • Only the own value of the source counts. The gateway takes encrypted_subject[<own OIN>] from the proof: the VI for consent:identity, and the VP for consent:pseudonym. The own decryption component of the source reads the value with the keys of the source.
    • The recipient must match. The decrypted value must name the own OIN of the source as recipient, or the gateway does not accept it. The key in the proof is not evidence. The value that BSNk signed is the evidence.
    • Three cases lead to a refusal, and the request then goes no further:
      • A form is missing, for example no VI for a source that is not on the BSN authorization list.
      • The value is for another recipient.
      • The query has a literal subject under a consent proof.
    • The gateway does not verify the proof again. The PDP verified it on the same request, and the gateway runs only after the allow.
    • Isolation is the control:
      • Only the source Inways reach the gateway (network source-gateways).
      • The gateway reaches only what serves the source (network sources).
      • The gateway publishes no port.
      • The gateway accepts only the request shape that the PDP judged: POST, one path, a JSON body, and no query string.

    Considered options¶

    1. The source gateway decrypts after the allow (chosen).
    2. BSN resolution in the PEP (ADR-0010). The PEP becomes a middlebox that transforms data in shared infrastructure, with a BSNk call in the query path.
    3. The source gateway calls BSNk Transform per request (ADR-0011). BSNk transforms only while the citizen is logged in, and a query comes later.
    4. Transformation in the PDP. Policy is not a data pipeline (F-37). With this option, the PDP holds BSN authority.
    5. The gateway verifies the proof again. This option adds no protection, because a consumer holds real proofs. The protection is that no request reaches the gateway without the allow of the PDP (F-79).

    Consequences¶

    • The query path has no central party and no BSNk. Only the source holds BSN authority, as P-10 requires.
    • "After the decision" holds only while nothing other than the Inway reaches the gateway (REQ-81). The compose networks do this. A Kubernetes deployment needs a NetworkPolicy or an equivalent. In demo v0.9.0, the Helm chart has no such policy.
    • A nonce does not bind a value to one consent. That binding is not built (F-79).
    • A source keeps the decryption keys of an older key version while proofs for that version are valid (AV-09).
    • A source must get its keys in advance, as a step of admission (BSNK-09, onboarding keys, #467).
    • The gateway is a processing. It writes LDV records for the decryption and the forward (ADR-0026).
    • In the demo, the three sources share one OIN and one decryption component. The mock does not encrypt. Production needs one decryption component per source.
    • Two parts are not built: a source API that answers on a pseudonym (#474), and a pseudonym for the consumer itself (#478, Q-01).
    • The gateway is separate from the HTTP handler. For this reason, the gateway can move into an Inway plugin later.

    Traceability¶

    • Requirements: REQ-04, REQ-17, REQ-21, REQ-79, REQ-80, REQ-81, AV-09, BSNK-04, BSNK-07, BSNK-08, BSNK-09
    • Findings: F-06 (closed), F-30 (resolved in demo), F-37 (resolved in demo), F-79 (open)
    • Open questions: Q-01 (partly answered)
    • Demo increments: SL-02 (done), SL-22 (done), SL-51 (done)

    ADR-0034: An integrator connects under FSC delegation, and the consent binds the represented party¶

    • Status: accepted
    • Date: 2026-11-02
    • Satisfies: S04, S05, P-01, D-11
    • Deliberation: REQ-106, F-20, F-73, Q-12, and demo #379, PR #464, docs/integrator.md
    • Implemented in:
      • lib.rego: the acting party and the represented party.
      • engine.rego: the mandate check.
      • dvtp_helper.rego: the consent binds the represented party.
      • autosign.rego: the delegated grant.
      • onboarding service.go: integrations and acts_for.
      • dvtp-onboarding.yaml: the PIP pull.

    Context and problem statement¶

    A consumer (afnemer) can let a software party, the integrator, call the source for it. The consent binds a consumer. The policy compared the dienstverlener_oin of the consent with the FSC peer that calls. An integrator breaks that assumption (F-73). The integrator calls, but the citizen gave consent to the consumer.

    The integrator acts as processor for the consumer (Q-12, AV-06). The integrator must not get access of its own. It must act only for the consumers that registered it (REQ-106).

    Decision¶

    The decision has four parts:

    • Transport. The integrator connects over an FSC DelegatedServiceConnection grant (grant type 3). The consumer is the delegator and signs the contract.
    • Contract admission. The contract decision of the source admits a delegated grant only if the admission register has that integration. If not, the decision refuses with DELEGATION_NOT_REGISTERED (ADR-0015).
    • Mandate. The admission register records per integrator the consumers and the rules that it acts for (integrations, pulled into OpenFTV as acts_for). At request time, every delegated call needs a mandate for the represented party and the granting rule:
      • If the mandate is missing, the engine denies with INTEGRATOR_NOT_REGISTERED.
      • If the register data is missing, the engine denies with INTEGRATOR_REGISTER_UNAVAILABLE.
      • The engine applies this check to every rule. No rule can leave it out.
    • Consent binding. The consent binds the represented party. That is the FSC delegator, or the calling peer if there is no delegator. The consent gives the integrator no mandate.

    Considered options¶

    1. FSC delegation plus a mandate in the admission register (chosen).
    2. The integrator calls with its own direct grant. The source then sees only the integrator. Either the consent binding fails, or the integrator gets access of its own.
    3. The integrator in the consent proof. With this option, the citizen also consents to the integrator. FR-DvTP v0.9 does not ask any more to tell the citizen about the integrator. It stays open whether the proof names the integrator (Q-46).
    4. No integrator role (the earlier TO). Real consumers use software parties, so the design must say how they connect (F-20).

    Consequences¶

    • The integrator gets a separate admission and acts as processor (AV-06).
    • In demo v0.9.0, a mandate has no validity period. It ends only when the register entry changes.
    • The admission register is also a request-time input, in addition to a contract-time input. A suspended consumer with a valid contract can still query directly. REQ-110 covers that gap.
    • OpenFSC puts the delegator in act.sub and the connecting peer in sub. That is the reverse of RFC 8693. The demo reads the values as OpenFSC writes them. An upstream issue is due.
    • The autosign input has no grant data. For this reason, the contract decision admits the pair, but not the direction of the delegation. The mandate check at request time closes that gap.
    • In the demo, the path is opt-in (make demo-integrator, peer …1100).
    • One point is open: can policy read the FSC Peer ID as the OIN of the consumer (Q-68)?

    Traceability¶

    • Requirements: REQ-106, REQ-48, REQ-61, REQ-62, REQ-110, AV-06
    • Findings: F-20 (closed), F-73 (closed)
    • Open questions: Q-12 (answered), Q-46 (open), Q-68 (open)
    • Demo increments: none

    ADR-0035: W3C Trace Context is the correlation key, and the FSC transaction ID is recorded next to it¶

    • Status: accepted
    • Date: 2026-11-02
    • Satisfies: P-12, S09, D-08
    • Supersedes: ADR-0019
    • Deliberation: REQ-55, F-67, F-41, and demo PR #366 (#365), PR #329
    • Implemented in:
      • ldv-client/tracecontext.go: the rule and the order.
      • consent.rego: the status lookup carries the trace.
      • The entry components consumerhttp.go, eudi-adapter/main.go, and asi-provider tracing.go.

    Context and problem statement¶

    An auditor must follow one request through the consumer, the PDP, the source gateway, the source, and the consent register (toestemmingsregister). Three standards record parts of the request:

    • LDV (processing records) and the ADL (decision records) require that a component takes the incoming trace ID over unchanged (LDV §3.3.1, W3C Trace Context §3.1).
    • FSC-Logging gives every FSC transaction its own transaction ID, unique per transaction (§3.4.1.1).

    ADR-0019 used one value for both. That choice breaks in three cases (F-67):

    • A caller sends its own traceparent.
    • One processing calls several sources.
    • The request takes an extra FSC hop, for example the status lookup of the PDP.

    FSC forwards traceparent on the data path. Only the AuthZEN call of the Inway to the PDP drops it (F-39, F-41).

    Decision¶

    The decision has four parts:

    • Every GBO component takes the trace ID unchanged from the incoming traceparent. If the caller is in the same trace, the component sets the span of the caller as parent. The component sends traceparent and tracestate on every outbound call.
    • The order of sources is fixed: traceparent, then Fsc-Transaction-Id, then X-Request-Id, then the ambient span, and then a new trace.
    • The Fsc-Transaction-Id never replaces an incoming trace. A component that starts or receives an FSC transaction records the transaction ID next to the trace ID. It records the ID as span attribute gbo.fsc.transaction_id, and in the ADL as adl.fsc.transaction_id.
    • If an entry component receives no traceparent, it can tie its new trace to the UUIDv7 transaction ID that it mints. This part of ADR-0019 stays.

    Considered options¶

    1. W3C Trace Context, with the transaction ID next to it (chosen). This option follows LDV, ADL, and FSC-Logging at the same time.
    2. The transaction ID equals the trace ID (ADR-0019). F-67 showed that this option fails.
    3. A custom correlation header. Not chosen: LDV mandates W3C Trace Context.

    Consequences¶

    • One processing has one trace ID and several transaction IDs. Logs and traces join on equal identifiers. They do not join on time stamps.
    • The consent status lookup carries the trace and the transaction ID of the request. The LDV record of the register lands in the trace of the request.
    • Separate units of work keep separate traces. The consent_id joins the consent issuance and the later query. A trace does not join them (F-16).
    • Behind the FSC Inway, the ADL record has its own random trace and no adl.fsc.transaction_id. The cause is that the Inway sends neither header to the PDP. A reader finds the record through the request headers stored in it. The fix is upstream in open-fsc (#369, ADR-0036).
    • A private consumer must send trace context and record the transaction ID (AV-01).
    • In demo v0.9.0, the operational logs of bron-sidecar, eudi-adapter, and asi-provider carry no trace ID.

    Traceability¶

    • Requirements: REQ-55, REQ-71, REQ-72, AV-01
    • Findings: F-16 (closed), F-39 (resolved in demo), F-40 (resolved in demo), F-41 (resolved in demo), F-67 (resolved in demo)
    • Open questions: none
    • Demo increments: SL-07 (done), SL-38 (done), SL-50 (exploration done, build delivered)

    ADR-0036: The ADL is the authoritative record of authorization decisions¶

    • Status: accepted
    • Date: 2026-11-02
    • Satisfies: P-12, S09, S05
    • Deliberation: REQ-71, F-53, F-63, F-72, and demo PR #337, PR #373 (#332)
    • Implemented in:
      • docker-compose.yml: the ADL is required in every profile.
      • adl-reader.sql: the SELECT-only reader.
      • authz.rego: what the record carries.
      • dev-portal-backend/adl.go: the lookup by transaction ID.

    Context and problem statement¶

    The PDP produces two decision logs:

    • The Authorization Decision Log (ADL), which OpenFTV writes to Postgres.
    • The console decision log of the embedded OPA, which goes to Loki.

    The design did not say which log is the audit source (F-53). The Logius standards family has three records with three roles (F-63):

    • The ADL for decisions.
    • LDV for processings (ADR-0026).
    • FSC-Logging for transport.

    A PDP decision is not a processing, so it is not an LDV record.

    Decision¶

    The decision has four parts:

    • An ADL record holds every PDP decision. OpenFTV writes the record to the Postgres database ftv_adl. The PDP does not start without this database, so the ADL runs in every deployment profile.
    • The ADL record is the audit source for authorization decisions. Contract-acceptance decisions are ADL records too.
    • The console decision log of the engine is observability. Nobody cites it as the record of a decision.
    • A reader gets a SELECT-only database role (adl_reader).

    Considered options¶

    1. The ADL as audit source (chosen). It is a standard record with an access model.
    2. The console decision log as audit source. Not chosen: it is a log pipeline that can lose or sample lines, and it has no access model (F-53).
    3. Per-field detail in the reason of the record. Not chosen: the Inway returns the reason to the consumer (F-72).

    Consequences¶

    • The record carries only {allow, reason}. On a deny, the reason is the code for the consumer (FIELD_NOT_PERMITTED, ACCESS_DENIED, COVERAGE_UNVERIFIABLE <subcode>, and more). The per-field rule codes and the step trace are only in the console log (REQ-06).
    • The record has these known gaps:
      • The record does not name the policy version (policies: 0, REQ-59).
      • The record does not hold the consent-status answer (adl.core.information) or the configuration (F-72).
